speakeroldname: Hon. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
speechtext:
May I ask the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K.
Maclean) if there is any report accompanying the volume which he has laid upon the table of the House and which is supposed to contain the classification of the various positions in the Civil Service, or if that report is the only thing which will be handed to the members to enable them to form an opinion upon the changes which are being made?

The report of the classification already laid upon the table of the House comprises substantially all the information that will be given to hon. members. There is, however, a report from the so-called efficiency experts to the Civil Service Commission.
Hear, hear.
" So-called " is the proper word to use.
Hear, hear.

I did not mean to reflect upon the experts by so designating them, as I have a very high appreciation of their work. There is a report from the experts to the Civil Service Commission, which report deals with the general principles involved in their method of classification, and which, I think, will be submitted to the House in a few days by the Civil Service Commission. I cannot promise my hon. friend that that report will be laid upon the table of the House before the second reading of the Bill is moved.

I think my hon. friend is- in error in supposing that there is something very strange and unfathomable about this classification. It is a very simple matter.
It is too simple as it stands.	.

It does not pretend to set up a single new position in the public service of the country. I hope my hon. friend will change his mind, because I trust to get the Bill and the classification through Parliament in a few hours, as there is no reason why it should be delayed at any length.

As regards selecting a committee to consider this Bill-I do not know if this is the proper time to put the question or not-is it the minister's intention to hand-pick the committee, or is he going to pick the committee from hon. gentlemen interested on both sides?
Some one will have to pick the committee and I should be glad to have the assistance of my hon. friend in regard to the matter.

On motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine), Bill No. 148, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (transfers and mortgages of ships) was read a second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-transfers, mortgages, or transfers of mortgages of ships to be subject to approval:

Is .there anything new
in the law, or is the old law being re-enacted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the resolution was before the committee, I explained that the object of this Bill is simply to put into effect two Orders in Council, one passed on March 9, 1915, and the other on October 9, 1917. These Orders in Council, when the Peace Treaty is signed, would, so I am informed, become invalid, and the object of this Bill is to have similar legislation to that passed by the Imperial Gov-

ernment in 1915, entitled The British iShips Transfer Restriction Act, which is valid for three years after the declaration of peace. That same clause is in the Bill now before the committee. It is necessary to have such a law in order that, if any owner of a ship wished to have a transfer of registry or a transfer of mortgage, he would have to apply to the Minister of Marine to get it.
Can the minister give a concrete case?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In the case of a
ship built in Montreal, from which city the hon. member and I come, if the owner wished to have American or French registry, in the past he would merely have to go to the registrar of the court of Montreal to obtain it. Now he will have to apply to the Minister of Marine.

Is this absolutely necessary? In our part of the country, where vessel transfers are quite frequently made, every bill of sale or mortgage has to be drawn there, sent to Ottawa, submitted to the department and receive approval before we can do business at all. Is not that a policy of centralization? You have your collector of customs, who is the registrar of shipping in the port of Sarnia. Why can he not receive instructions so that we may, as in the old days, take a bill of sale or mortgage to him, or have a transfer approved by him and entered in the registry of shipping and kept in that port? I think that shipping registrars in the different ports could be instructed to carry out the regulations just as the department would here. It would save time and considerable expense, not to mention a great deal of correspondence. One of the rules of the department is that no mortgage may be drawn except upon the specific form furnished under the Shipping Act, and with extended periods of payment for the mortgage it is an absolute impossibility to put the terms of repayment in the form furnished. It has to be changed and typewritten forms must be used, and at the present time the department absolutely refuses to accept any form except that furnished. I cannot understand the reason for this. The matter might be simplified if the registrar of shipping in the port were allowed to carry on the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Orders in
Council passed on the 9th of March, 1915, and the 9th of October, 1917, respectively, under the War Measures Act of 1914, were

absolutely necessary in order that Canada might conserve and control her own shipping. England in her wisdom-and she is a good example in the matter of shipping and shipping laws-saw fit to pass what is known as the Transfer Restriction Act. It was passed in 1915, to be operative for three years after the war, in order that Great Britain may be assured that none of her shipping would get into foreign hands. That Act enables her to conserve her own tonnage. Canada is simply seeking to do what the United Kingdom has done, and it would be very unfortunate for this country, with so much ship construction in progress now, if we did not pass this law. There is a remarkable shortage of shipping. Canada not being able to export one-quarter of the freight offering, and if we allow these Orders in Council to lapse and do not pass this Bill it will simply mean that we shall have no control whatever over our shipping. A man could go to a registrar and ask for the registry of any country he liked, and it would be given without question. Under the provisions of the Bill a foreign company applying for the registry or transfer of a ship will have to come to Ottawa and make application to the minister, so that we can investigate the bona fides of the applicant and decide as to the advisability of giving the transfer. We cannot have these rights granted through the registrar of the port, and if this Bill does not pass we shall revert to the position in which we were before the war, and transfers of ships will be made just the same as transfers of land.

The registrar is an officer of the department. Can he not be given instructions?
'Mr. BAIiLANTYNE: My department will have no instructions to give him unless this Bill is passed.

I have no doubt the minister is right in regard to some of the ships about which he speaks, notably steel ships. But if this' Bill goes through without amendments or a satisfactory guarantee a great many of the wooden shipyards in the country will have to close up business. The minister says this Act is in accordance with a similar law passed in the United Kingdom. Conditions in Canada are quite different from those that obtain in Great Britain, where there is enough business for themselves to keep their yards busy all the time. Most of the wooden ships being built in Canada are for sale and not intended for use in Canadian trade. In fact, for a number of years past the majority of wooden
ships built in the provinces have haid to go outside of Canada to obtain business. The minister is optimistic in the matter of what ships can do in Canadian trade. Well, I am not so optimistic and from my experience I know that we cannot expect sufficient business for a great many of our wooden ships. I would remind the minister that even his own marine had to go outside of Canada for business, and, indeed, was able to secure better trade outside. The provisions of this Bill will work a hardship on the shipowners in Canada, especially in the Maritime Provinces. A great many vessels are sold in foreign ports. A ship may go to Brazil or France, and an offer may be made the captain, who then telegraphs his owners. Sometimes such offers are made in the British West Indies, and if a sale is to be hoped for the owners must be in a position to telegraph immedi-, ately whether the offer can be accepted. If an owner is under the necessity of communicating first with Ottawa-and large bodies move very slowly, this being certainly" the case sometimes in the Marine Department, which takes a great deal of time to consider these matters-there will be no sale. We should encourage the selling of vessels outside of Canada if we expect to keep our shipyards busy. A great many men in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick when the war broke out and when Mr. Lloyd George made an appeal for ships, invested money in new shipyards, although some of them were already interested in old concerns. So far we have not received any returns on our capital, and if this Bill is made law and we are to be handicapped with unnecessary delays our business will be seriously prejudiced, for we shall certainly find it, to say the least, extremely difficult to effect sales with the United States or France if we have to apply to the Minister of Marine for permission to sell. In the past few years we have had some business with foreigners, although I should not use the word "foreigners" in connection with our Allies, France and the United States. Gentlemen from those two countries would give certain specifications for ships they required and prices would be fixed before even the keel was laid. Now, how can we shipbuilders in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick under this Act enter into a contract with French or American capitalists when we do not know whether the minister will allow us to transfer a ship after she is built? I would urge on the minister my apprehension that if this Bill goes through without the guarantees, the

shipbuilders of the Maritime Provinces will be driven out of business.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I may say to the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Buff) that I cannot agree with his argument that this will drive the wooden shipbuilders of the Maritime Provinces out of business; quite the contrary. The Government is just as anxious as is the hon. member for Lunenburg that all ships that can be built in Canada under our allied register, either wooden or steel, should be built here. There is no delay in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. All these requests are dealt with very speedily. If there was any blame it would rest on the shoulders of the minister, and I can assure the hon. member that I despatch such matters very quickly after ascertaining who the owners are. He mentioned the case of a wooden shipbuilder in the Maritime Provinces who got an order from France and who could not make the sale because he would be in doubt as to whether he could get registry or not until the ship was built. That is entirely contrary to the facts. Quite frequently men come to see me-there is one waiting for me now-to know if he can get register before he completes the deal. If an American shipbuilder, or any of our Allies, want ships built in Canada, they will be told that when the necessary very simple questions have been asked and answered, they can immediately get their registry. I am sure that in such times as we are now going through, my hon. friend from Lunenburg will recognize the necessity, in the interests of Canada, of the Government retaining control over shipping for at least three years after the war. Otherwise, we do not know what _tonnage, either wooden or steel, which is being built in Canada, will slip out of our control. I cannot agree with the hon. menlber when he says that we have to go outside of Canada to get trade. The fact is quite the contrary. As I said a moment ago, we could commence to move the products of the farm and of most of our industries, if we had all of our forty-five new ships in commission to-day. It would be an unwise policy for the Government to allow any of our ships, either wooden or steel, that are being constructed now, to pass under foreign control, or possibly into the hands of our enemies. This is merely a precautionary measure; it does not mean delay at all. Last year the number of transfers allowed on the application of both Allies and neutrals, was twelve, and the number of ships that applied for transfer of registry was 138. The hon. member will

see that we have already handled quite a number of transfers, and no one has complained about delay. I appreciated the fact that these matters must be dealt with speedily when they come before my department. No mortgage can be transferred or registry given unless the minister himself personally approves, and I can assure my hon. friend that I shall approve of these applications very speedily when they come before me.	.

The explanation given by the minister is fairly satisfactory. So long as there is no delay I can assure him that it will be satisfactory to the wooden shipbuilders but they must have immediate action and they must know before they build the ships whether they can sell them or not. I was in the United States about a month ago and I had previously been in correspondence with a gentleman in Boston who has a large amount of money that he wishes to invest in Nova Scotia ships. He would be willing to put $50,000 into ships built in Nova Scotia, as an investment. This was before I knew anything about this Bill and I told him there would be no trouble in arranging it because in the past people in the United States have had shares in Nova Scotia ships. The shares were owned by British subjects but the British subjects gave a mortgage in the name of the American citizen. When I discussed this matter with that gentleman he told me that he had $50,000 to put in ships in Nova Scotia and I told him there was no reason why it could not be done in the usual manner. If this Bill goes through, and if I understand the Bill correctly, Canada will lose that money. If I am right in my interpretation of the Bill this gentleman cannot invest this money in Canadian shipping because we would not be able to give him a mortgage for the money that he invests. Am I right in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will be able to give him the necessary transfer of mortgage. There is no difficulty about that. You will have to apply to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to get bis authority to give a transfer of the mortgage but there will be no delay or difficulty about the issuing of the mortgage. I am just as anxious as any hon. member to increase shipbuilding in Canada, altogether apart from what the Government is doing, and we will render every assistance to promote that object. But I am sure that hon. members will recognize that there is absolute necessity of Canada controlling her

shipping tonnage and she can only do that by asking people in these various countries to apply to the minister for a transfer of the mortgage or register.

My principal objection- to the Bill is that it is an unnecessary interference -with business, without accomplishing any good object. If the minister says that he is going to give -his consent to all applications the Bill is no good. He has now pledged himself to the House that if any Canadian citizen wants to sell his ship to an American he will give his consent and the citizen will have a free hand to do it. Then, what is the use of the Bill? If it is to be of no use and if the minister is going to give his consent under all circumstances, it seems to me to be an interference with business and to have no good purpose. It always takes time to get the consent of the minister, and very often difficulties arise. Why should we put on the statute-book a law which will be of no service to anybody? As far as the control of shipping is concerned, the minister is not now exercising control over Canadian ships. Canadian ships are used freely in the trade of the world without any interference on the part of the minister. The fact that they are under Canadian registry does not seem to help Canada in so far as getting freight carried is concerned because the Canadian shipowner can carry freight from the river Platte to Great Britain ot from the river Platte to France, or anywhere else -and nobody interferes. Unless the minister intends to go farther and say that no Canadian ship can sail outside of Canada without the consent of the Department of Marine and Fisheries or of the minister, I do not see that any good purpose will be served by creating this obstacle to business. The minister knows that he is not controlling freight at the present time; yet, it does not make very much difference because if a ship is afloat and seeking business, it is immaterial to it what flag it sails under. It makes a good deal of difference in times of war but in times of peace the American shipowner is just as willing to accept Canadian business as American business provided the Canadian business is better. Unless the minister intends to go another step further I do not see the need for putting this law on the statute-book.

Possibly it would help the situation if the minister would give a clear explanation of the circumstances under which approval would be given and the
circumstances under which approval would be refused. If the only object is to prevent our building ships and selling them to our alien enemies, if there .are to be any such in the future, I am sure we should all sympathize with it. But, I come from a section of the province of Nova Scotia where there has been quite a revival of the shipbuilding industry, as my hon. friend (Mr. Duff) has described. There is very great activity, there has been quite an improvement of the situation in -a business way and otherwise, but there is a fear now that the orders which have come there during war time may not continue. The view is expressed that we should encourage this industry by every means possible. If the minister could give us a definition of the class of application which he would accept and the class of application which he would be obliged to refuse it might help a good deal, because in the case of orders for new -ships, at all events, they could point to the conditions as defined by the minister in the House and that would have some weight. I entirely agree with what my hon. friend from Lunenburg -said as to the desirability of encouraging wooden shipbuilding in the lower provinces which has proved to be a very valuable industry in the last three or four years, and if we cannot help_ it along, we, at all events, should do nothing to obstruct it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I will be very glad to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) the information he has asked for, but before doing so I wish to state my position more clearly than possibly I have ,so far done in answer to the hon. member for Antigonish "(Mr. J. H. Sinclair). While 1 sand I would give authority to a citizen of the United States or to a citizen of France who wanted to get a transfer of mortgage or a -transfer of registry for a wooden ship,
I would not do so without making the necessary inquiries and satisfying myself as to who the people were that were applying for such transfer, but the necessary inquiries would be made by wire and speedily. There has not been any delay in these -matters since I have been Minister of Marine, and I do not see that any occasion for delay will arise in the present case.
In answer to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's I am pleased that he has asked -me to put the case in the way he did, and for his benefit I will state two concrete instances. Suppose citizens of our ally France asked for a transfer of registry or a transfer of mortgage. If the people

making 'the application were subjects of that country it would be granted immediately. On the other hand, the necessity of not taking these applications for what they purport to be without inquiry is illustrated by a case which occurred some months ago. One of the neutral countries applied for registry, but upon investigation we found that the vessel was intended to engage in enemy trade in the interest of an enemy country. The fact, however, that application had been made to the Minister oi Marine to get registry enabled us to prevent that ship, which was built in a Canadian yard and under Canadian registry, from passing into alien enemy hands. That is the principal object of this Bill, to see that none of our wooden or steel ships get into the hands of our enemies, and secondly to conserve our Canadian tonnage as much as we possibly can. Now here is a case which might possibly arise, although I do not say that it would: Take one of the ships that have been built by the Imperial Munitions Board and which that board may possibly want to sell to the United States or France. If we were very short of -essels, we might say: "No, we want to buy that ship ourselves." This Bill affords us the opportunity of looking first after our own interests and keeping our tonnage out of enemy hands.

I am very glad that we have now ascertained exactly what this legislation means, and if that be the minister's object I think, personally, he had better drop this Bill. He says that he does not want a Canadian ship to pass into the hands of an enemy, and I understand we are to have the Peace Treaty signed within a few days. Does the minister come before this Committee with the definite policy that after that Treaty is signed we are not going to do any business with those who have been our enemies in the late war, but that we are going to put obstacles in the way of business being done? Is that what my hon. friend means?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the hon. member will allow me-[DOT].
The question is one which can be answered in the affirmative or the negative. If the minister does not care to answer it I will assume that is what he means.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will answer the hon. gentleman as soon as he is finished.

If that is my hon. friend's attitude then it may be neces-

sary to explain to him that it means he is going to do everything in the way of preventing the payment of any of the enemy indemnities toy means of sea freight, because the only way in which the indemnities we are insisting upon the enemy paying can toe paid, is in goods, and so far as those goods come across the sea they must come in ships. If the whole abject of this legislation is to enable the minister to prevent our putting shipping facilities in the way of what he is pleased to still term enemy countries, then the economic effect will toe to put obstacles in the way of paying these indemnities. That will toe the meaning of his policy, 'that will be how it will work out in our future relationships with those countries. I have no particular use for our alien enemies, tout the fact is that under 'the Peace Treaty we have particular use for the indemnities which we demand they shall pay. Those indemnities can only toe paid in goods. Those goods can only toe brought in ships; and the minister -comes before the House with a Bill to perpetuate the powers given in war time by an Order in Council. That was very proper while we were at war, tout now that we shall shortly toe at peace the minister proposes to perpetuate the powers given under that Order in Council to the thwarting of our re-establishing of trade conditions, which means the thwarting of the payment of indemnities.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Michael Clark), as we all know, is not only a very loyal Englishman tout a good Canadian as well. Nevertheless, he has apparently overlooked what I stated in my opening remarks, that the Old Country-the country from which he comes and which very seldom errs, particularly in shipping matters, because it has had the experience of hundreds of years, has passed a Bill similar to the one we are considering declaring that it will hold control of the transfer of mortgages and of registries until three years after peace has been signed. Surely Canada cannot go very far astray in following the example of the United Kingdom in that respect?
But that is only part of my answer to the hon. gentleman. I am more concerned about the interests of our own country. To-day we are short of shipping, and I have no hesitation in saying to the committee that if I received an application at the present time from Germany, or Austria, or Hungary, for a transfer of mortgage or a transfer of registry, I would say "no." I do not know what our answer might be a

year or two years from now, but in view of the feelings which we entertain towards those countries, and the existing shortage of Canadian tonnage, I would be derelict in my duty if I allowed such transfer of shipping tonnage under Canadian registry which is so badly needed by the Canadian people, and I would deem myself unfit to be a minister of the Crown. Under the circumstances I am quite sure that no member of the committee desires that should be done. For my part I am anxious to safeguard as far as possible the interests of Canada. This Bill does not contain a single restriction that is calculated to injure Canada; every word and every sentence in it is intended to promote the best interests of the Dominion. In the explanations so far given I covered the ground sufficiently; I merely desire to say briefly that we desire the necessary authority to deal with the construction of ships in Canada, both steel and wood, during the reconstruction period which we estimate will last for a period of three years. When that time has elapsed shipping will of course be open just as it formerly was. As it is, I will place no barrier in the way of securing a justifiable transfer of registry or mortgage; the Department of Marine will act as speedily as it can in the matter, but I certainly will make no promise that at this time, and in view of the terrible war we have recently gone through, I will be willing to give a transfer of mortgage or registry to any of our enemies.

Might we reasonably assume-leaving out of the question the so-called enemies, and possibly after Friday next they will possibly be no longer classed in that category-that in the case of applications from the United States or any neutral government-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There will be no trouble at all.
There will be no objection?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None at all.

Then that removes to some extent the objection to this legislation. If the operation of the Bill was intended to be permanent I would entirely agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Michael Clark), but it is limited to three years and the policy which has been deemed proper in war time may be tolerated for a few months after the war. It is only that limitation that would make the Bill justifiable at all.

If the minister would agree to confine the operation of the Bill to alien enemy countries no objection could be entertained to it at all, but for my part I see very serious objection to the legislation in its present form as being likely to hamper business. Let us say that a case occurs, such as the hon. member from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) referred to, where an outside capitalist, from the United States or some other country, wishes to contract with Canadian builders for the construction of a ship. The agent of that capitalist arrives in Canada, but he is not going to deal merely with one firm, he makes approaches to all the firms that are open for business. All of them will be hampered because they cannot foretell what will happen in the course of the negotiations. Men want to know where they stand, particularly in the making of a contract. They cannot say: " We will build this ship for you and give you a good title to it at a certain date," unless they know where they stand. If there are half a dozen firms negotiating with the same party the minister will have a lot of trouble on his hands and he will not be able to satisfy anybody. That is my principal objection to the Bill. If the minister could see his way clear to confine the Bill altogether to alien enemy countries, I think all our opposition to it would be withdrawn. The minister says that it does not hamper business; but it does. The penalty is severe-a $5,000 fine and five years imprisonment. I would ask the minister if he could not amend his Bill to make it apply to the nations he refers to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have dealt with
dozens and dozens of cases such as the hon. member for Antigonish has mentioned. I can only say again, that if any man or any number of men want to transfer to any allied or neutral countries, they can do so by telegraphing to my department. I would simply wire back and say, " We will give you registry for the United States, France, (Norway or Italy,"-as the case might be -" provided, of course, that the company is not going to be foreign controlled." There will be no hampering of business, because we have been all through this for years and have not had the slightest difficulty at all. I can assure hon. members that there will be no delay and no restriction of trade, and undoubtedly it is a wise piece of legislation to put through at this time for the reasons I have already given.

I understood the minister
to say, in reply to the hon. member for

Antigonish, that he would give permission for the transfer if the ship was not to be controlled 'by a foreign company. If a man in the United States or France buys a ship, he will control it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I should have said if the ship is to be under alien enemy control.

Of course, this would not
apply to the Dominion of Newfoundland?
Mr. BAiLLANTYNE: No.

But while we are discussing this Bill I might call the minister's attention to the fact that we have had a great deal of difficulty in the last three or four years in getting vessels transferred from the Maritime Provinces to Newfoundland. We have had to get the consent of the department, and in some cases have had to submit to a great deal of delay and inconvenience both in the selling of new as well as of old ships. I remember a particular case last September; a fishing schooner went into St. John's, Newfoundland,	and	the captain	had an
offer for her. He telegraphed to the owner-by the way, he was a good friend of the Government-and this gentleman came to me and ashed if I would telegraph to Ottawa for permission to transfer the ship. It took me three [DOT] weeks to get the transfer arranged. At first the department absolutely refused to grant permission If this occurred in the case of new vessels we would not be able to do any business. But if the minister will give us his word that there will be no trouble, and that immediately on receipt of a telegram from anybody in Canada the matter will be looked into and permission given or not given, I think there is not much harm in the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
In answer to my
hon. friend, I have a letter of thanks and appreciation from the late Colonial Secretary of Newfoundland, Mr. Squires. He came to Ottawa on the morning train to see me about the transfer of a large number of wooden ships from Canadian to Newfoundland registry, and he was able to return by the afternoon train. I not only gave him, between trains, the transfers he wanted, but I also had the
12 noon, pleasure of having him to lunch.
When he returned to Newfoundland I got the thanks of his Government for the speedy way in which I had handled the matter. The Colonial Secretary told the

Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he expected to be in Ottawa several days; instead of that he was only in the city three hours. That is the policy we have followed in the past, and that is the policy we intend to follow in the future
How does the matter stand with regard to the transfer of ships to Newfoundland registry; do we still have to apply to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
There will be no trouble?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No trouble at all.

I have one or two words to say to the hon. minister. He carefully avoided any explanation of how he proposed to get the goods from those enemy nations who have to pay war indemnities, and he sdemed to lay down a policy which, from my point of view, is utterly bad on two grounds. My hon friend referred to me as an Englishman. Well, I have a great deal of admiration for England. I do not know the particulars of the British measure, but I would like to give my hon. friend and the Government a piece of advice, and that is to imitate England when she does good things, and not when she does bad things. I have not unlimited confidence in the Government that is ruling England at the present moment. Neither, as far as I can see, have a large number of constituencies in which byelections have taken place. There is a certain species of lower animal, known as the mimetic species, that have the power oi imitating other objects, animate or inanimate, to save themselves from their enemies. I sometimes feel that this is a mimetic Government. If ever we attack a proposal, it is supposed to be sufficiently defended when we are told that it comes from England or from the United States. That is not quite a good thing to an Englishman who has just a little Scotch blood in him. I do not want to elaborate this point too far, but I am going to deal svith the points my hon. friend raised. He seemed to think it was a sufficient defence to his Bill to say that it came from England. Two years ago daylight saving was defended on exactly the same grounds, and this Parliament carried a measure giving it effect without discussion almost. This year this same Parliament voted against it by two to one. Why? Not because it was English or American, but because they tried it and found it bad. So much for my hon. friend's English precedent. I will go into

his English precedent a little further in a moment.
I view this legislation not only with suspicion and distrust, but with hostility, on two grounds. In the first place, I do not think that we can afford, in Canada oi all places in the world, to be forever at war with the peoples whom we have fought and beaten. My hon. friend says that I am an Englishman. When a boy in England, after a bout of fisticuffs outside a public house, I have seen the victor help the fallen man to his feet, take him inside, and stand him a drink. That is what we mean when we speak of an Englishman. When he has his spite out he forgets it, if those with whom he has fought will allow him to do so. I say it would be a most unfortunate thing if this Government, after the war is over, is to perpetuate feelings of international hatred and jealously-the very feelings out of which war arises. I argued in this House on the Military Service Act that the only ground on which I would de-fenc^ conscription was that we were adopting it to kill conscription. The only ground on which I could defend war was that we were at war to end war. And if we are ever to indulge the sentiments of international hatred and suspicion, then it is because those sentiments are forced upon us. So much for that side of the question.
Economically, this legislation is bad from my point of view. My hon. friend utterly failed to touch the point that I raised with regard to how we are going to convey goods from enemy countries if we pursue a policy through our Marine and Fisheries Department of restricting our traffic with those countries.
I hope that my hon. friend gets the point. I wonder how far he would restrict his trade with those countries? Let us suppose that peace was signed. My hon. friend is a business man; I do not know what class oi goods he handles-at least, I have no right to mention it here. But suppose that in his capacity as the head of a business firm he is hard pressed to make his business go. I hope that he will never be in those circumstances, but it is a fact that we are all anxious, in the short time between the cradle and the grave, to do all the business that we can; let us get rid of any cant and humbug in this connection. Suppose that during the three year-period of the reconstruction of shipping operations with what were enemy countries, my hon. friend's firm was offered a large order by a reputable concern in any one of the enemy countries, at a time when we were trying to forget the
war and to reconstruct our country and oui business. I would like my hon. friend to tell me whether he would say: Oh, we were at war with the Germans a year ago; I really could not fill this order. Would he take that attitude? If every business man in Canada did his business in that way, what would be the result? But I am very suspicious of my horn friend. I know what kind of business man he is; I do not think he would put upon himself, even for the three years, a commercial self-denying ordinance of that kind. If he would not, then commercially his Bill is bad, because he has himself avowed that its object is to reconstruct commercial intercourse with those who were our enemies.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is aware that I am no longer active in business ; rightly or wrongly I am devoting all my time and attention to the public position that I now occupy. The people who are carrying on the business that I formerly managed will have to decide the question raised by my hon. friend. What is before us now is this Bill and the question whether it is in the best interests of Canada. I have gone into it fully and have nothing more to add on the subject. I am sure that the committee is satisfied that there is no restriction of trade about it; on the contrary, it is designed to promote and facilitate the shipping of Canada and to see that it is in proper hands. If a year or two from now any of our present enemies made application for a transfer of registry or of mortgage, I would bring the matter before the Government for decision. This Bill does not absolutely shut out such a transfer; it will be for the Governor in Council to decide questions of that kind.

The minister heard on a previous occasion the member for South Cape Breton and Richmond (Mr. Butits) and myself discussing the question of the return of ships and shipping that had been commandeered for the purposes of the war. We pointed out that many of these ships had not been returned and (that the circumstances revealed in connection with their detention did not seem to be altogether creditable to those concerned. Have these ships been returned to their former contracts or pre-war charters? If not, is the Government assisting the companies, and those who are immediately concerned, to get these ships back ? Quite a number of ships were under contract in the early days of the war with the Nova Scotia Steel

Company, and with the Dominion Coal Company for the carrying of coal to the ports on the St. Lawrence. They had contracts for terms of five, tten or fifteen years at what were regarded as good rates, but at rates which were low compared with those to which we have become accustomed during the war. These ships were put into the service of the British Government at high rates, and, naturally enough, the owners are anxious to continue them in that service as long as possible. But those who had them under contract are anxious to get them back at once, because without them their business is crippled, and the business o.f the people who are interested in the products of these large companies is seriously affected. If the Government can do anything to expedite the return of these ships to their former charters and contracts, it should be done as speedily as possible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am, perhaps, somewhat more familiar with recent aspects of the subject referred to by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) than' is the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), because thait subject has had the attention of myself and of other Canadian ministers on the other side of 'the ocean on many occasions during the last five or six months. I do not intend ito speak very fully upon it at the moment, because negotiations have been proceeding and representations have been made quite recently; in fact, before coming to the House this morning I drafted a communication on the subject which will go forward to-day. I think that if the member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) was aware of some of the communications that have passed and of some of the representations that have been made, he would not be inclined to regard the Government of Canada as purely a mimetic government. As a matter of fact, we have taken very strong issue with authorities on the other side of the ocean as to certain aspects of the course which has been pursued. It is not desirable that I should speak more fully on this aspect of the question than in the words I have just used. The leader of the Opposition can be assured that no effort that could properly be made has been wanting and that the representations which have been addressed not only to the British Ministry of shipping, but also to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, have not been lacking either in vigour or in firmness.

I would like to supplement what the leader of the Opposition has said, though I take it for granted, as the Prime Minister has told us/ that every effort is being made to deal with the situation. The importance of this mattef to various interests can hardly be overestimated. It is of great importance to the coal interests of Nova Scotia; and that is a far-reaching interest that affects not only the coal companies, but also the employment of a large army of men. It affects also the interests of the Government of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It affects the revenue of the province.

Yes. It affects largely the interests of the city of Montreal as concerning the St. Lawrence coal trade. Unless these ships are released from their engagements by the British Government and placed at the disposal of the coal trade, I am afraid that we shall have difficulty in supplying the city and port of Montreal and the neighbouring sections of the St. Lawrence with the coal upon which they rely for their industrial enterprises. From every point of view the matter is one of very great importance, and I am very glad to receive the assurance of the Prime Minister that the Government have been doing and will do everything they can with a view to securing the return of these ships.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may say to the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) that in view of pending negotiations I shall consider the advisability of making a somewhat fuller statement to the House than I have made this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I know that the Prime Minister and his colleagues who have been overseas recently have done everything (possible to get these ships in order that they may be put into the coal trade again. When I was overseas last summer, by making many, many visits to the Minister of Shipping, I was able to get free the ships "Turret Court" and "Turret Cape," but of course, they were under Canadian registry. When ships are not under Canadian registry, we have not the authority to deal with them as effectively as if they were, but I am fully aware of the serious lack of tonnage to bring coal to Montreal, and with the Prime Minister, I shall be very glad to lend whatever aid I can.
Were not all those ships that were commandeered, if not under Canadian registry, under Canadian charter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot say positively. They were not all under Canadian registry, but they were, so far as I know, under Canadian charter, and really they ought to he returned to Canada. It is a shame that they have not been, but as the Prime Minister has stated, he will take every step possible to get them back as soon as he can.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-forfeiture on owner ceasing to be a British subject, or becoming a foreign controlled company.

Does the minister regard this clause as necessary? It reads:
Where, after the passing of this Act, any person who is the owner or mortgagee of a British ship registered in Canada ceases to be a British subject or becomes a foreign controlled company, that ship, or, in the case of a mortgagee of a ship, the interest of the mortgagee, shall be subject to forfeiture.
That is going pretty far. Supposing a Canadian moves to the United States and becomes a citizen of that republic, he forfeits the ship he happens to own. Is this forfeiture absolute, or is there a way of escaping it? I was struck with the severity of the clause, and I want to hear from the minister why he thinks it is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As the hon. member will notice, that is already covered by Part 1 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1894.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-duration of Act:

May I call attention to the wording of this clause? It may be sufficient; it may not. Before the Royal Assent can be given to this Bill, in all probability, peace will be reached by means of the treaty, although it may not have been proclaimed. The present war is referred to in this Bill, hut by the time this Bill is receiving the Royal Assent, there may be no present war. It is enough to call the attention of the draughtsmen to the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I should hardly think the suggestion of the hon. member would affect the matter, for this reason, that peace cannot be proclaimed until three of the Allied nations shall have ratified the treaty. Therefore, it is, I think, perfectly clear that we should still be technically in a state of war for some weeks and probably
months after this Bill will have received the Royal Assent.

The Prime Minister
is counting on an early prorogation.

Will, in all cases, the
peace treaties have to be ratified by the various Parliaments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is a matter of domestic concern within each country. As regards the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister has given an undertaking that the peace treaties shall be submitted to the British Parliament before ratification, and we intend to pursue the same course here with respect to all the treaties. We shall have them laid before Parliament in order that they may be considered by Parliament before we shall authorize ratification on the part of Canada.

I do not know if I made myself very clear. I understand the peace treaties will be signed by the plenipotentiaries, and as regards Canada, we are bound by the signatures of the Prime Minister of Great Britain and his colleagues who attend the Peace 'Conference. Then the treaties will, as a matter of course, be sent to the various Dominions, Canada included, and be considered by Parliament, not for the purpose of ratification, if I understand well, but simply for the purpose of passing judgment on the treaty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The ratification is an executive act. Parliament would not ratify the treaty; Parliament might be concerned in the passing of legislation which the Peace Treaty would render necessary. I do not think it is the intention of any Government within the British Empire to ratify any Peace Treaty as an executive act without first consulting Parliament and giving Parliament an opportunity to express its opinion thereon.

As peace will be concluded in a month or two, I would move that this clause be changed to read:
This Act shall continue in operation for three years.
Cutting out the words " during tbe present war " and " after the conclusion of peace." It will make only a difference of a month or so.
Mr. J. H. 'SINCLAIR: That is three years from the date on which the Bill receives the Royal Assent.
Yes.
Amendment agreed to.

Mr. iLEMIEUX: 1 understand the object of the Bill, but will it affect only alien enemy ownership^of ships, or all foreign owners, whether belonging to a friendly power or to an enemy power.
Mr. BA-L-uANTYNE : All foreign ownership.

I understand some
friendly powers are going to organize a line of steamers between Canada and Rumania.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Every one, whether belonging to an enemy country or to a friendly country, has to apply to the Minister of Marine.
Section as amended agreed to.
Bill reported, and amendments concurred in.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue) moved the third reading of Bill No. 53 (from the Senate), to amend the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this Bill receives its third reading I would like to call the attention of the House to certain features of it with which I dealt on a former occasion and which I feel are not thoroughly understood. If they were, I do not. think the Bill would have reached its present stage in the form in which it is now before us.
1	would direct attention to the clauses relating to registration and license fees in the Bill as amended, and which will hit retail druggists severely, and to subsection
2	of section 2 which, as amended, reads:
For the purposes of this Act the proprietor of a proprietary or patent medicine shall be deemed to be the manufacturer thereof.
That means that in a great many cases retail druggists will legally be manufacturers of the medicines which they sell but which may have been manufactured by one of the wholesale patent medicine manufacturing firms. Under section 3 every manufacturer, who will be a retail druggist according to the previous section, shall, before offering any medicine for sale, procure from the minister a numbered certificate of registration for each proprietary or patent medicine he proposes to offer for sale. He will have to pay $2 for each certificate, and another section imposes a license fee of 81 for each preparation that
[Mr. A. K. Maclean.!
is sold. Large wholesale manufacturing firms will simply pay $2 for each article they manufacture, which will mean practically nothing to them, while the retail druggists will have to pay the same registration fee for each article which in a great many cases they will not manufacture, and an annual license fee of 81 for each preparation sold. In order to satisfy myself of the fact that it will bear heavily on retail druggists, I made inquiries of a number of druggists, who gave me information that confirms my contention that it will. One druggist tells me that 17 preparations of his will come under this Act. He will have to pay, therefore, registration fees amounting to $34 and annual license fees amounting to $17. Another druggist sells four preparations, and another fifteen. The latter has just started in a new business and he informs me that if he carries the line of goods he had in his last business he will sell thirty-five preparations, which will mean $70 in registration fees and $35 in license fees. Another druggist has ten preparations and another six. From a city druggist I get the information that city druggists will have to pay in the way of license fees an average of from $5 or $10 up to $00 or $100 per annum. I am sure it is not the intention of the Act to impose these fees on retail druggists who after all are receiving the minor profits in the patent medicine business. I regret the Bill is worded as it is. but I believe it is not yet too late to make the necessary change, and I hope the minister wall take the matter further into consideration and modify the Bill so as to relieve retail druggists of these heavy costs. It may be said that $10 or $20 is not much, but it is a great deal in these days. The reason for imposing these fees is, of course, to defray in some measure for the cost of administration, but I think the men who should pay for the cost of the administration of the Act are the large manufacturers. The great burden of the cost should be imposed on them because they can best bear it. If the Bill passes as it is, in a year or -two it will fall into the same condition as the last Patent Medicine Bill and become a mere dead letter, incapable of being properly enforced owing to the opposition and dissatisfaction among retail druggists throughout the country. It is far better to have a law which can be .'strictly enforced than one which will meet with determined opposition all round. I trust the minister will give this matter his

earnest consideration 'before the Bill finally passes.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: In submitting this motion; the minister exercised his right to speak. Under our rules a reply is not permitted, but owing to the peculiar circumstances of the case, I presume the House will give unanimous consent for the minister to make reply.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Before my hon. friend Replies, I would like to draw attention to a resolution passed by an association of ladies in the West in which is denounced the use of alcohol in certain preparations.
I wonder if my hon. friend will take action in regard to the resolution passed by this association? As he accepted the amendment moved by my hon. friend from Beauce (Mr. Beland) concerning the use of opiates in drugs, will he permit to be sold in future what remains in stock, in the various drug stores, of drugs that may he poisonous in that they contain opiates? I refer to preparations for the use of babies. Surely my hon. friend should prevent the sale of such drugs that may be in stock.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Immediately this Act goes into force, the further sale of these prohibited drugs will be prevented, and the loss will fall upon those druggists who have them in stock. I shall he glad to take into consideration the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Steele) and if I find that .an amendment is necessary I can overtake the Bill in the Senate. The matter he suggests was discussed very fully by the committee who were of opinion that you could not differentiate between the small manufacturer and large manufacturer of patent medicines. Many local druggists sell very largely their own patent medicines, and if they want to avoid payment of the tax all they need to do is print upon the bottle or wrapper the formula showing the ingredients of the medicine.
I do not think it would be fair to say that the large manufacturer of patent medicines must pay a tax different from that imposed on the small manufacturer of perhaps similar medicines. I am doubtful whether there should be any such thing permitted as the patenting of drugs at all. I hope we will reach the time when everybody who discovers a medicine of value will be very glad to reveal the formula to the world. I am rather inclined to have very little sympathy with anybody who is engaged in the patent medicine business.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: No respectable man would keep secret a medical discovery which would cure any one.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The enforcement of this Bill would have prevented the use of antitoxin and such preparations as that, which at first were kept secret.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I have studied something of the history of medicine, and I do not know of any remedy that is a cure for anything that was ever discovered by a physician anywhere that was kept secret, with the exception of Salvarsan, a cure for syphilis, which was discovered by Elrich. He kept it secret and patented it.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Then, we are spending time for nothing. Drug therapy seems to have become a lost art. Doctor Huxley said of young students: They work to pass, and outraged science gets her revenge. If my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce consults the records of malpractice in the United States he will find that the cases are in the following proportions: Physicians 60, druggists 10, and patent medicine manufacturers 4. Therefore, I must ask the minister to give more consideration to the druggist's part of this matter. If he had accepted my suggestion the other day he would have wiped out the patent medicines that are absolutely no good. He has given no protection to the public and in this connection I know what I am talking about.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I did not answer my hon. friend's question correctly. I remember reading a resolution this morning from some ladies' organization at Regina, I think-objecting to the use of alcohol in

medicine. Possibly they did not go that far because it is impossible to compound medicines without alcohol. I think that probably the gist of the resolution was that we should prohibit an excess of alcohol in drugs without sufficient medication. (Medicine might be so compounded that the liquid would be potable and could be used as an ordinary alcoholic beverage. The Bill provides that the advisory committee can prohibit the sale of any drug containing alcohol that is not sufficiently medicated. I shall discuss the point raised by my hon. friend behind me during the day personally or privately.
Mr. lLEM'IEUX :	What penalty is provided for breaking the law in the case of drugs containing opium?
Mr. A. K. M,A CLEAN: There is a general penalty clause.
Mr. PETER McGIBiBON: When this Bill was up at first I asked the minister if he could give us any information as to the cost of administering the Act. I would like to know if he has any further information.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We are not in committee; this is on the motion for the third reading of the Bill and I would suggest that there should be some attention paid to the rule that only one speech is permitted from each hon. member.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am unable to give my hon. friend (Mr. P. McGibbon) that information now.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the third time and passed.

>On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean, Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, the House went into Committee on the following resolutions, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring' in a measure to amend The Canada Grain Act, chapter 27 of the statutes of 1912, and therein to provide,-
1.	That in lieu of the provisions of section
102 of the said Act, it be enacted that there shall be a board to be known as the Board of Grain Appeal, to consist of three members who must be expert and experienced in the inspection of grain to be appointed by the Governor in Council;	.
2.	That

(a)	each member shall hold office for ten years, but may be removed for cause, and shall retire upon reaching the age of seventy years;
(b)	a member upon expiration of his term of office, if under seventy years of age, shall be eligible for reappointment;
(c)	one of such members shall be appointed iby the 'Governor in Council as Chairman of the Board; two members shall be a quorum;
(d)	the salaries of the members shall be such as are fixed by the Governor in Council;
(e)	the fees to be charged by the Board of Grain Appeal shall be set by the said board on or before the first day of September in each year, and shall be approved by the Governor in Council.
(f)	the members of the said board shall devote the whole of their time to their duties under the Act and shall not accept or hold any other office or employment.
(g)	no member or officer shall, directly or indirectly, hold any interest in any corporation subject to this Act, nor directly or indirectly deal in or be financially interested in grain or hold any interest in any grain elevator or warehouse or in any partnership, corporation or business engaged in the grain trade or. in the transportation or storage of grain;
(h)	the members and such officers as may he directed shall before acting take and subscribe an oath of office in prescribed form.
(i)	the said board shall hear all appeals from the decisions of the Chief Inspector on samples of grain, as provided' in section 101, and perform such other duties as are prescribed by the Governor in Council by regulation or otherwise;
(j)	the offices of the said hoard shall be in such place as the Governor in Council may direct, but for the purpose of better considering any particular appeal, the board or any of its members duly appointed in any special case by the said board may hold sittings at any other place in the division.
3.	That in lieu of the provisions of subsection seven of section ninety-five of the said Act, it be enacted that in the month of August in each year, stock shall toe' taken of the quantity of each grade of grain in the terminal elevators; if a surplus in any grade of grain is found in excess of one-half of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain received in the elevator during the crop year, such excess surplus shall be sold annually toy the Board of Grain Commissioners and the proceeds thereof paid to the said board. Such proceeds shall be applied towards cost of the administration of The Canada Grain Act in such manner as the minister may determine on the approval of the Governor in Council.
4.	That the provisions of section 101 be amended so as to provide that appeals from the decisions of the Chief Inspector, on samples of grain respecting which the grading is in dispute, shall be to the Board of Grain Appeal.
5.	That in lieu of the provisions of section 103 it be enacted that the Board of Grain Appeal may make by-laws for the better carrying out of the business of the Grain Survey Board of any district in the Division, and for the establishment of a schedule of fees for survey services.
6.	That the provisions of section 104 be amended so as to provide that a survey board with offices in Calgary shall be established and

appointed for the district of Calgary, and that the provisions of section 101 ("Grain Survey Board " being substituted for the " Board of Appeal") and 103, as amended, shall apply to such survey hoard.
7.	That sections 101, 102', 103, and 104 as proposed to be enacted, shall come into force from such date as may be prescribed by proclamation of the Governor in Council.
8.	That the provisions of section 119 be amended to provide,-
(a)	that all licenses, issued under the Canada Grain Act shall expire on the 3lst August in each year;
(b)	that the Board of Grain Commissioners shall fix the amount of- bonds to he given by the different persons specified in said section and by primary grain dealers; and license, control and regulate the trimming of all grain at Fort William and Port Arthur
(c)	that the said board, in its discretion, may accept security of persons, Arms or corporations to whatever amount and in whatever form shall be deemed necessary by them in lieu of bonds ;
(d)	that any person who engages in any business for which a license is required under the said Act, without first obtaining such license shall be guilty of an offence and liable, on summary conviction, to a penalty of not less than five hundred dollars and not exceeding two thousand dollars and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or to both fine and imprisonment.

23. That the penalty prescribed by section 24 5 he amended to provide for a penalty of not less than twenty-five dollars for the first offence, a penalty of not less than two hundred and fifty dollars or two months in jail for a second offence, and to a penalty of not less than five hundred dollars or three months m jail for a third offence.

The Bill proposed to be founded upon these resolutions will contain perhaps two important amendments. The balance are not of such importance. The principal features are those providing for the establishment, of a board o.f appeal in Western Canada in substitution for 'the board of surveys, as I think it is now called. That is the body which hears appeals from the inspectors of grain in the western provinces. Very strong representations have been made to the Government by western interests to establish this hoard of appeal, particularly the producing interest. This is not a measure absolutely free from doubt as to the advisability of the creation of the board and I am quite .content that Parliament shall have every latitude possible in reaching a proper conclusion in regard to it. It is proposed that the board should consist of three members and that they shall not engage in any other business than the hearing of appeals from the inspections of the various graiii inspectors of the grain producing provinces.
The other important feature of the Bill is that which provides for a limitation^ of what is called the "overages" in connection with the terminal elevators. Section 2 of the Bill will provide:
That in the month of August in each year, stock shall be taken of the quantity of each grade of grain in the terminal elevators ; if a surplus in any grade of grain is found in excess of one half of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain received in the elevator during the crop year, such excess surplus shall be sold annually by the Board of Grain Commissioners and the proceeds thereof paid to the said Board. Such proceeds shall be applied towards cost of the administration of The Canada Grain Act in such manner as the minister may determine on the approval of the Governor in Council.
The Bill will propose that the proceeds of the overages shall go to the Grain Board for the purpose of meeting the cost of administration of the Canada Grain Act. I am not absolutely wedded to that proposal; it may be sounder in principle that these revenues shall go to the Consolidated Revenue Fund account, hut there is a great deal to be said in favour of it.
The Bill will also provide that any surplus in excess of one-half of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain shall he
fMr. A. K. Maclean.]
sold annually. There will be doubtless a variation of opinion whether or not this is a proper average. It has been represented to me by some, that one-quarter of one per cent is a proper average. Others say one-half; while still another class suggests that the proportion should be midway between one-quarter and one-half. It is perhaps difficult to determine what is the proper percentage because the producing interest, that is the farmers in the West, object to the establishment of a cash tariff for elevators. The elevators in the past have counted upon deriving practically the greater portion of their remuneration for elevator services from the overages which they receive.
Did I understand the minister to say that the producers object to a cash basis for overages?

I said that I understand the producing interests of the West are opposed to the absolute elimination of overages, and the substitution of a cash tariff for elevator services. That is my impression. There was a delegation of representative men fronl the West before me, perhaps two months ago, and I put that question to them, and was told very emphatically that the farmers do not at present care for the idea of a cash tariff. I may be wrong in that view.

I think it is just the reverse; the farmers want each tariff to pay for itself. They want to know what each tariff costs them. They do not want any of the tariffs to be mixed up with overages, or anything of that kind; in their opinion, each tariff should stand on its own basis.

I cannot hear my hon. friend very distinctly, and perhaps we misunderstand each other. I am merely stating my view that the wheat growers in the West do not want the absolute elimination of any overages at the elevators, and would not be sympathetic towards a purely cash tariff for elevator services. That is my view and I do not think I am wrong in it. If that view is correct it is very difficult to determine what should be the exact percentage of overages which should be left with the elevator company. I might say that during the past year an audit was made of the overages obtained or secured by the different terminal elevators of Canada during a period of five years at the instance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the report disclosing the results was laid upon the table some considerable time ago. I assume that the facts therein

stated are known to hon. gentlemen, and therefore I need not go into any of the details of the report. '
Other provisions might more profitably be dealt with when the Bill has been printed and probably it would be better to defer consideration of every question and every principle involved until after the passage of the resolution. We are providing also for more severe penalties against persons who engage in the handling of grain in any manner without having first received a license. Hon. gentlemen from the West will know that in recent years some dealers having a track-buying license have-engaged in the grain commission business without having furnished the Board of Grain Commissioners with a bond, and after purchasing grain have failed to pay the persons from whom they made the purchase. We are endeavouring to prescribe severer penalties for such violations of the Act. I do not think I need trouble the committee with an explanation of other sections of the Bill, because ample opportunity will be given hon. gentlemen to discuss many matters relating to the grain business upon the second reading of the Bill. Several members earlier in the session had resolutions on the Order Paper involving a discussion of matters relating to the grain industry, but they were not reached and I promised the hon. gentlemen referred to that upon the second reading of the Bill there would be the widest latitude to discuss everything that relates to the grain business in the West.

When the Bill comes up for the second reading it will be still later an the session, and I personally would not like to take up time by any extended remarks upon this question. I would prefer to speak now upon the resolution, unless the minister is absolutely opposed to it, because the later we get in the session the more impatient of discussion the House becomes. I do not think it will tend to shorten matters to postpone the discussion until the second reading, although I have personally no intention of putting myself on record twice.
