Now just a few figures regarding the earnings of this company. These earnings are all based upon the capital basis which has been applied to all these cases by a committee of expert auditors who investigated the matter. They allowed the elevators $50,000 for each million bushels capacity. The 'Grain Growers' Company rent the elevator, I think, from the Canadian Pacific for which they paid the company, if I remember rightly, $68,000. Anyway, they paid a rental equal to about six per cent on the capitalized value of the elevator. Now omitting screenings and overages this company earned in those five years an average of 7.73 per cent, which is a very reasonable and fair earning. Adding the screenings, but excluding the overages, they earned 11.81 per cent on'the average of five years. Including the screenings and overages, the earnings were 18.85 -per cent. The point in all these figures that I have given is the abnormal earnings of all these elevators because of the screenings and the overages which they illegally take from the farmer. And why do I say "illegally?" Because in the Grain Act, I think in clause 126, you will find it clearly set forth that wherever dockages- are made for screenings the elevator company shall account to the shipper, the owner, or the farmer for them. Now, as a matter of practice, it was found by the auditors who investigated all these companies that they never did notify the shippers of these screenings or dockages except when it was demanded of them, and they knew nothing about wfiat the overages would amount to until they weighed up at the end of the year and then made the discovery, and of course they did not know to whom they be-

longed. These overages occur largely out of dockages made in the way I have mentioned.
Now, I want to draw the attention of the committee to the returns secured by the Grain Growers' Company-I give their figures as a sample, and I have others as well -on the capital invested.
What is the name of that elevator?

The Grain Growers' Grain Company, I think they call it now the United Grain Growers. I am under the impression that it is Canadian Pacific Railway elevator No. D. Now the company in 191617 earned a total of something like $446,000. The operations of the elevator yielded $238,000; screenings, $51,000; overages, $156,900, The expenses were operating and management, $136,000; depreciation, $29,000; and rent, $68,000 Deduct $234,000 expenses from the earnings of $446,000 and we have a net result of $212,000. Now it must be remembered that the working capital estimated by the experts as being needed for this elevator was $100,000. Of course, the Grain Growers' Company may say this is not a sample of their general business, but in all these calculations the same operating capital has been allowed by the experts, -which in this case gives earnings of something like 211 per cent. In connection with its operations this company, in common with all other companies, sold grain on option before the overages actually occurred. In other words, they anticipated that overages would occur and they sold, or dealt in grain stored in their elevators.
Will the hon. gentleman state what proof he has of that statement?
I have an audited statement, in my hand which was laid on. the Table a couple of months ago, and which I had an awful time getting from the minister who has charge of this Bill.
I do not think so.

Well, I had to dodge about quite a bit before I got it, but I thank the minister for his courteous treatment of me in the long run. I find that this company lost in options in the year 1916-17 the sum of $24,055. This amount, of course, is added to the expenses and deducted from the earnings leaving something like a profit of 187 per cent on the operation of that elevator. This is not an abnormal profit for elevators. This is the profit which all the other elevators shared in and it was not peculiar to the Grain
Growers' elevator. For instance, we have the Port Arthur Elevator 'Company which has overages of $185,000, $51,000, $50,369, $112,716, and in the year 1916-17 overages to the amount of $388,000.
Now, what I want to get through the minister's head is this: He is putting in the Bill one-half of one per cent of the amount of grain handled through these elevators as a cure for these abuses. My point is that not only should we prevent these elevators from carrying on these abuses and keeping these overages, but that every dollar taken out of overages for the last five years contrary to the Grain Act should be paid back into the treasury of Canada either for distribution to the proper owners or, if that is impossible, to. be used for the public welfare.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me a question?
One at a time.
What would you do in the case of a shortage?

My hon. friend advances an argument, which is the only argument that is presented from time to time: What would you do in regard to a shortage? As a -matter of fact, shortages occur only in very few cases and are deducted from the total overage. I have not the " red " figures, as they call them, but the allowance for shortage is mighty small. The point is this : the large elevator could so operate as not to create either a surplus or a shortage. It may be that we have to make some small allowance for that; but what I am complaining of is that one-half of one per cent will virtually perpetuate the abuses'" which have been continuing for the last seven or eight years, and it is altogether too much. If you allow anything at all, one-tenth of one per cent would cover it very easily, or more than cover it. I ask the minister, therefore, that before he insists upon the quantity fixed in the Bill going through he should put some good actuary to work on these figures and let him figure the percentage. Any good accountant would come within a few bushels of what is necessary to protect these companies against the possible shortage which, by the way, rarely occurs.
Now I wish to point out this: Another practice carried on by all the elevators-
I won't say all of them, but by a good many of them-at the head of the lakes is this, they pay their officials a bonus on the amount of overages created in these elevators from year to year. I do not like to

use strong language but after studying the matter with the utmost care I see nothing for it but to say that the bonus is given for the dishonest handling of the grain in these elevators. There is no man who studies this case carefully but must be convinced that these overages are abnormal, that they are unreasonable, and they are utterly unfair to the shipper. And when I find one company paying six officials an average salary of $7,000 a year-some get a little more, and some a little less-or a total of $40,000 in salaries and bonuses, that is altogether out of proportion to the business of the elevator. This practice is a pernicious practice. It has been indulged in for a very, considerable time and we, as a Parliament, owe it to the shipper, to the farmer, and to the dealers of the country that it should be stopped absolutely. Had I had the privilege of moving a resolution which has been on the Order paper ever since the session opened and to which I endeavoured to speak half a dozen times, I had intended to move that these elevators should pay back to the owners, or pay over to the exchequer of the country, the amount of overages accumulated during the last four or five years. I am not going to delay the House with any further lengthy remarks in connection with this subject, because the session has now reached so late a period that I would not be justified in doing so. I have merely cited a few figures from the report of this special committee of auditors. The Government has this report in its possession and it would take very little effort to work out what is necessary to cover any possible shortage. Certainly, to make the figure one-half of one per cent is simply perpetuating the abuse which has been carried on for a number of years, instead of making that abuse illegal. If I had my way I would make it a very serious offence to retain any overages, and also do everything possible to reduce the overages which have occurred, as they have occurred during the past few years.

The hon. gentleman
stated that the dividends paid by this company, I have forgotten to whom-were apparently seven per cent, but on many transactions they had a percentage of 211 per cent pn capital invested. Do the hon. gentleman's figures show what became of that surplus? Who got that very large amount?

'I presume that went
into the general fund of the company, I could not tell the hon. gentleman that.
I might explain, Mr. Chairman, that 
these figures are the figures of a special committee of auditors appointed by this Government, under an Order in Council, to investigate all the terminal elevators at *the head of the Lakes. Now that my hon. friend has reminded me of it, I might say that a proposition has been before this country for years that the Government should take over and operate these elevators. It has been a subject of comment not only regarding these elevators, but with respect to privately owned elevators that they have been used during the past few * years to increase the cost of living. Now regarding what my hon. friend says, all the elevators referred to have been computing their earnings, and so forth, on a systematic basis. They have allowed for each elevator a working capital of $50,000 per million bushels capacity, which is considered by them after careful investigation to be ample. Now in the case of nearly every elevator I find in analyzing these figures that the elevators have either paid the whole, or a very large proportion of the total cost of their plant out of these earnings extending over a period of from seven to eight years. In the case referred to by my hon. friend, and which I dealt with a moment ago, the Grain Growers Company, they operate in a very large way all over the country and have many different branches, but the operation of an elevator is quite a simple process to figure put. They rent an elevator and *pay $68,000 for it. The commission .of expert auditors allowed them ,$50,000 per million bushels capacity, as they do in every other case, or a total, I think, of $100,000 working capital upon which, of course, interest is allowable, but the earnings of the elevator, taking out your expenses-rental and so forth-and leaving them with a working capital of $100,000 was, as I have said, 187 per cent after deducting the lossses on options on the market, and of 211 per cent without these losses.
Mr. ORER.AR: The subject that is under discussion this afternoon is one of very great interest to the country-in fact, this is applicable to anything that has to do with the handling of the grain of Western Canada. I followed with a good deal of interest the remarks of my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. IManion). I think he raised no objection to the amendments to the Grain Act, which are now under the consideration of the committee, excepting the point that the Board, of Grain Appeals should be located in the city of Fort William. It may be of interest to members of

the House, who are not, perhaps, closely familiar with the methods of handling our grain, to give a word of explanation as to what is really intended by the amendment to the Act providing for a grain appeal board. Our grain handling system in Canada is, I think, without exception, the best method of handling grain that can be found anywhere in the world. The foundation upon which it is largely built is our grain inspection system, whereby
4 p.m. the grain, as it comes from the farmer's hands, is inspected, classified accordingly, and sold abroad on the inspection certificates of the chief grain inspector. Now the chief grain inspector is located in the city of Winnipeg and all the members of his. staff are there. There are subsidiary branches at Eort William and Port Arthur at the head of the Lakes, and in Calgary, Moosejaw, and, I believe, in Saskatoon. The inspection system as we have it to-day depends almost entirely on the eye test of the inspector. Provision is made for taking a sample of grain from a car that is shjpped, in such a w-ay as to ensure that it will be a fair average sample of the car. That sample is taken to the inspection department, passed upon by the inspection officials, and the grade given to it, and that grade governs, It has happened in the past that deficiencies or defects occasionally arose in that system, and to further improve it the proposal has been introduced into these amendments to the Act providing that a Board of Grain Appeals shall be formed to which there may be an appeal taken from the decision of the chief grain inspector in respect to the particular grade that may be given any car of grain. This has worked out very successfully in Minneapolis, and I am free to say that our farmers in Western Canada have asked pretty insistently for this for several years back.
Now the point my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) makes is that this Grain Appeal Board should be located in the city of Fort William. My contention is that it should be located in the city of Winnipeg for the reason that the sample upon which the inspection is first made is taken either in Winnipeg or before the car reaches that point. Here the sample is passed upon by the chief inspector or hi3 officials in Winnipeg, and consequently if there is to be any value in a Board of Grain Appeals that board should be located at the point where the inspection is made. It is not intended that fresh samples shall be drawn from ears, otherwise there is no
need for an appeal board. The very intention and purpose of this legislation is that there shall be an appeal from the judgment of the chief grain inspector, or his officials, upon any particular sample of grain that a farmer or dealer might wish to have referred to the Grain Appeal Board. Consequently, that being the case, the Grain Appeal Board should be located where the sample is first secured and where it is readily available.

The hon. gentleman knows that in Minneapolis the Board of Appeal have provided for a fresh sample. He objects, at least I take it from his remarks that he does, that a fresh sample is not necessary in Canada. Is that the hon. gentleman's contention?	'

I was just coming to that . point. There may be an occasional case where it is necessary to secure a new sample from the car. In such cases I will admit the hon. gentleman has a valid argument for locating the Board of Grain Appeals at Fort William, but I say that such cases will be very rare. I believe that in Minneapolis in actual experience, and in Duluth also, that has proven to be so.
We will probably further improve our existing system by providing for duplicate sampling of cars, which obtains now in the Minneapolis market. Outside of this, the hon. gentleman from Fort William had very little criticism to offer of the amendments that are proposed by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I wish now to say a word or two as to the observations of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) who has, I am very glad to say, suddenly developed an alarming interest in, and friendship for, the prairie farmer. The hon. gentleman has not always exhibited that interest in the welfare of the prairie farmer, and naturally I am delighted to see such a manifestation on his part.
His criticism was directed mainly against what he called overages in terminal elevators, and concerning which there is a provision in the amendments proposed by the hon. minister. I regret that, perhaps for lack of time, the hon. member from Vancouver did not stated the facts altogether correctly to the Committee. I at once acquit him, let me say, of any desire to intentionally mislead the Committee; but his study of the question, Mr. Chairman, has been very elementary indeed, and he has simply picked out of a report here and there a few facts upon which he bases general conclusions that are entirely misleading.

Terminal elevators are warehouses, and, consequently, are supposed only to store grain for shippers and customers. But every man, Mr. Chairman, who knows anything at all about the handling of grain knows this fact, that you cannot operate a terminal elevator or a country elevator or for that matter any other elevator, where grain is handled in bulk, and have your outturn correspond identically with what you put into the elevator. That is an absolute impossibility. The Grain Act provides, and very properly so, that the owners of terminal elevators shall be responsible, as warehousemen, for every bushel of grain that is put into them. They have got to account for it. Not only that, but the provision is so strict, Mr. Chairman, that under regulations of the Board of Grain Commissioners for every car of grain unloaded into a terminal elevator there is issued what is called a terminal elevator warehouse receipt. That receipt is registered in the registry office of the Board of Grain Commissioners, and when so many bushels of any particular grade of grain are shipped out of the elevator, warehouse receipts corresponding to that amount have to be surrendered to the registry office of the Board of Grain Commissioners in order that they may keep accurate and absolute tab on the proceedings.
The.hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) made the statement that these overages have been illegally taken. I would just point out for the information of the Committee, that those overages have been taken with the knowledge and approval and consent of the Board of Grain Commissioners, the body created under this Grain Act to especially regulate the handling of grain in this country. If illegal why has the Board permitted it? I will tell you in a moment why they did it. Consequently when the hon. member for Vancouver leaves the impression on this Committee-as I think he did this afternoon;-or, at any rate, it was the only inference that could be drawn from his remarks,-that there has been a condition of affairs in Fort William approximating robbery, he is leaving an impression that is altogether contrary to the facts.
I stated a moment ago that it is impossible to operate an elevator, whether at Fort William, in the country, or anywhere else, and have your out-turn correspond exactly with what you. put in. That is a well-known fact. I have stated also that the owner of a terminal elevator warehousing grain is responsible for every bushel of grain that goes into that elevator. Not only so but he is responsible for every

bushel of grain of a particular g-ade that goes into the elevator. In other words, if I, as a terminal warehouse man, put 100,000 bushels of No. 1 Northern grain in my bins and if the inspection has been any way lax, the inspection department has for example allowed more moisture in the grain than should be permitted for No. 1 Northern, and the grain goes out of condition, I nevertheless am responsible to the Board of Grain Commissioners for 100,000 bushels of No. 1 Northern, and in that event I have to go into the open market and buy the grain necessary to make up the deficiency. Those are facts that were not stated by the hon. member for Vancouver in presenting his so-called facts, and in order to get an impartial survey of the situation they should be stated.
Now, how do the overages arise? Naturally, when the superintendent of an elevator is conscious of the fact that his elevator is short on any grade at the end of the season, or it is short on the total amount of grain put in, and his company has to go into the market to buy that grain to mane up the deficiency, he uses every precaution to insure that his elevator comes out right. When discussing this matter with the Board of Grain Commissioners years ago I stated to them, "You guarantee me against loss from shortages in my elevator, and you can have every bushel of surplus. But as long as the elevator warehouseman is placed in the position that he must make good every bushel of shortage that occurs in his elevator, then you cannot justly take away from him the right to participate in any surplus there may be." And that principle, Mr. Chairman, is recognized in the whole administration of the Grain Act, not only in the operation of elevators in the country but everywhere else.
Indeed, it is a comparatively easy matter to secure a surplus in an elevator if your handling is large. The hon. gentleman- I do not know what his motive was- directed particular attention to the Grain Growers' elevator in Fort William. I may say that in one season when- the crop was large we handled 28,000,000 bushels of grain through that elevator, and the amount of profit-to which the hon. gentleman has referred, I was going to say, pathetically, or at least in a tone of voice that indicated his extreme interest in the matter-[DOT] amounted to only a fraction of one cent per bushel on the stuff handled. The rather harrowing inference that the hon. member threw out in his remarks, that the making of this profit added to the cost of living, appeared to me to be ridiculous, and would

appear ridiculous to the hon. gentleman himself if he gave the matter a little thought.
I commend the step that is taken by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce in the amendment which he has brought down; and it may be that the existing system is not an ideal one. My own view is that the Government should frankly guarantee the elevators against shortages, place them upon such a basis that their remuneration shall toe confined to the cash tariff that they charge, and then appropriate the surplus. But that throws the risk of shortage in the elevator upon the Board of Grain Commissioners, and that is a risk that they very naturally do not wish to assume. Moreover, if these surpluses are entirely taken from the elevators, unquestionably it would mean an advance in the handling charge from three-quarters of a cent a bushel to at least li cents a bushel. In no grain handling centre in North America are the rates for the handling of grain through terminal elevators as low as they are in Port Arthur and Fort William.
As to the question of screenings, I regret that the member for Vancouver did not state the facts clearly. It is true that screenings come from the cleaning of grain, but there is a regulation of the Board of Grain Commissioners that where more than 3 per cent of screenings is cleaned from a farmer's car, the grain merchant handling the screenings has to make a separate return to the farmer for the value of them. Only in cases where the percentage of screenings taken from the car is under 3 per cent is no. return made.
Is there any regulation in the Grain Act respecting surplus of grain which corresponds to that with regard to screenings which go back to the farmer?

There is no such provision, because in my judgment, and, I am sure, in the judgment of the Grain Commissioners, it would toe impossible to work out any regulation that would permit that. A small allowance per car is made for loss in unloading-an allowance of 30 pounds per car ' for invisible shrinkage-and a portion, at any rate, of any surplus the elevator secures comes from that source. But a separate return is made for screenings where the screening is over 3 per cent, and in that case a charge is made to the shipper for cleaning the grain. The tariff for receiving grain in the elevator, unloading it, elevating it, binning it, and shipping it out again
if shipped within fifteen days, is three-quarters of a cent per bushel. In cases where a separate return is made for screenings an additional cleaning charge is made, but where no separate return is made for screenings-that is, where the screenings are under three per cent-no charge for cleaning is made. In other words, the elevator operator takes the screenings as his pay for cleaning the grain; and that practice has prevailed all down through the years. I quite appreciate the fact that there is possibility of an abuse growing up in this regard. But if the Government is not prepared, through the Board of Grain Commissioners, to assume the responsibility for any shortage that may arise in these elevators, then in my judgment the minister is taking entirely the correct course in permitting the elevator to rdtain a small portion of any surplus that may arise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
With regard to the question where the Board of Appeal should be located, I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar) that because the first inspection takes place at Winnipeg, and because that is where the chief inspector resides, the Board of Appeal should be located there. As a matter of fact, the chief inspector used to be at the head of the Lakes and should be there now; he should not have been taken away to Winnipeg. The business is all done at the head of the lakes. It passes through Winnipeg, and if there is any dispute about the quality of the grain a neiw sample should be taken. The car is only a short time in Winnipeg, and the sample may be defectively drawn; the only procedure that is fair to the farmer is to resample. But the cars stand on sidings at Port Arthur and Fort William, and there is delay incidental to that rolling stock. If the minister will consult the convenience of the railroad people and of the public generally he can come to only one conclusion, and that is that the Board of Appeal-as the Board of Grain Commissioners did recommend- ought to toe at the head of the Lakes; that it ought to be at Fort William. I may tell the minister that when Port Arthur and Fort William unite on a thing, it must be right.
Then, there is the question of overages. The minister is to be congratulated for cutting down these overages to at least one-half oJ one per cent. I was hoping, to use a vulgar phrase, that he would "go the whole hog." If a return to the elevator company of three quarters of a cent a bushel is not

sufficient to provide for any falling off of the grain, increase that amount, but let us be fair and square with the drain Act, which makes it absolutely illegal for terminal elevator people to deal in wheat. Yet, by virtue of the method which we have been pursuing, we have, in an indirect way, been giving the elevator people the right to take at least 3 per cent of the carload, clean it over again, and get that much to the good.
If the practice is illegal, why has it been permitted bjr the Board of Grain Commissioners?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I do not say that it is illegal; if it was illegal, it would have been stopped; but it is contrary to the underlying principle of the Grain Act. It has been held by some judicial twist of some person to be legal1, but it is contrary to the underlying principle, namely, that those terminal elevators should not speculate in wheat.
They do not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They should handle the grain from the shipper and send it on its way to the market. What is going to be the effect if you abolish this overage and dockage? These terminal elevators, with the exception of three or four, will go out of business, and they will all become private elevators. They will all at once begin to deal in wheat as they ought to be doing, as hiany private elevator companies are doing there, buying wheat from sample and grading it as they can and selling to a mill as they do at the place where the wheat finally reaches in England. That would be a benefit to the farmer, who will get more for his wheat when a sample market is established. The grain can be worked together, and perhaps a better price can be obtained, ajid he will not lose his dockage of 3 per cent. Private elevator men would buy the whole carload and they would be all competing one against another, so that the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) would have the principle he has advocated so strongly for, namely, free trade.
The question of screenings has been a continuous source of trouble -at the head of the lakes. If the screenings are to go 3 per cent up, to the owner of the elevator, there is an interest there that should not exist. If the elevator owner is paid simply the price he ought to be paid for cleaning the wheat a great deal of controversy will be removed and possibly a desire to get ahead of somebody else.
[Mr. Keefer.)

When the Acting Minister ol Trade and Commerce brought in his resolution this morning I could not but think that he was introducing this proposed legislation under duress, having in mind the statement made during the Budget debate by an hon. member from the West, that they had put the gun up to the Minister of Finance and compelled him to create three new government positions. We gather now, from the debate, that there are two interested parties; we have, first, Fort William and Port Arthur, which apparently are united in a campaign to open this new office in the twin cities. They are doing that upon instructions from their Board of Trade, because I hold under my hand- and I suppose every hon. gentleman has a copy-a circular letter put out in May by the members of the Fort William and Port- Arthur Grain Exchange urging the passing of this legislation. The Committee will note that no person has as yet made any real complaint against the present system of the Board of Appeal. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has given his blessing to the idea of this new board, but he has made no real complaint against the present system of appeals. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), if I understood him aright, stated that the Board of Appeal was constituted by certain members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. If that were correct, it would not be an ideal system, but my hon. friend is apparently wrong in his information. Article 102 of the Manitoba Grain Act provides that the Survey Board shall consist of twelve members, six of whom shall be appointed by the Board of Trade of Winnipeg, two by the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Manitoba, two by the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan, and two by the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Alberta, so that one-half of the members of the Grain Board are appointed by the Ministers of Agriculture of the three provinces which are particularly interested in grain. If there be anything wrong with those six gentlemen, if they have not the proper qualifications, then the remedy should be with the Ministers of Agriculture of the several provinces. My hon. friend from Fort William and Rainy River advances an argument in favour of locating at Fort William and Port Arthur, because he says that the milling is all done there, and that there is no milling at Winnipeg. As a matter of fact, there is a larger milling capacity at Winnipeg and St. Boniface,

I think, three times the capacity that there is at Fort William, where there is only on* moderately-sized flour mill, the Ogilvy flour mill.

There are two statements which the hon. member made in which he misquoted me, and I know he has no intention of doing so. He said that I stated that the present Appeal Board-really it is a survey 'board-is comprised of members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. I did not mention the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. I said that the appeal was put before the Survey Board at Winnipeg, which was made up of a number of Winnipeg merchants, at their head being Mr. Searls. In the second place, I did not say there was no milling at Winni-[DOT] peg. I simply said that, as regards handling shipping and milling grain, there were better facilities at the head of the Lake* than at Winnipeg.

The inference is that the
hon. gentleman tried to create the idea that the Survey Board was comprised of Winnipeg Grain Exchange men. As I was proceeding to say, there are large mills at Winnipeg. There is a large mill at St. Boniface, a large mill at Keewatin and a large mill at Kenora. I am not going to enter into an argument as to whether this board should be at Winnipeg or Fort William. My contention is that it is an unnecessary expense, that it is creating three jobs for some people. I do not know who are making applications for these jobs, but I should like to point out that it is contended that these three gentlemen should be expert grain men. That was the -contention when the members of the Board of Grain Commissioners were appointed, but }vho were appointed by the Government of which Sir Robert Borden was the Prime ^Minister? The Government appointed Mr. .Staples, a very good fellow. -Everybody who sat in this -House with Mr. Staples liked him very well, bu-t he was an ardent politician; he played the game fair and played it for all it was worth. He never pretended to have any expert knowledge of grain except that he was a good farmer. Then they appointed Mr. Leslie Boyd, another good chap. He was a lawyer of the city of Montreal; he was President of the Conservative Association, and, I think, once or twice he was a candidate for the Conservative party. Those were the qualifications of these expert grain men. Having that in mind, I wonder who is going to be appointed this time-. Will it -be an expert grain man? Will it be a man who is experienced in law or in theology? I do not know.

The Bill will provide that he will be an expert in regard to grain.
Mr. R'OBB: Will he be an expert in law or theology or grain? If the -Government are not satisfied, if there is complaint against the present system of the Appeal Board, ithat is to say, six members appointed by the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, the handlers of the grain and six members appointed by the Ministers of Agriculture of the three .Prairie Provinces.
Would it not do to appoint this grain commission as appeal board ? They have not very -much to do and no one will accuse them of being overworked. We are told they are expert grain men, and as their offices are in Fort William that will satisfy gentlemen there and add no more expense to the country. I am opposed to the resolution because it is imposing an unnecessary burden on the people. There is a suspicion that the real intention is to gratify the ambitions of Fort William, on the one hand, and on the other to -create good fat jobs for friends.

Let me assure my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) that the people who are asking for this are not holding a gun at anybody's head. They have been trying to get this thing done for the last five or six years. The people who produce the grain that furnishes the business for all these elevators are the ones with whom this idea originated, and not the people of Fort William, Port Arthur or Winnipeg, or the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. The president of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange was sitting in the gallery this morning and I had a long talk with him. They are not asking for the board, and may have even told the minister that perhaps it is unnecessary. So that if is not the grain interests that are seeking this. As a matter of fact, they would probably get along better without it. The people that are asking for it are the producers of grain, in order that they may get a fair deal in the grading of their grain. The grain will have to carry the expense. If a car is appealed, the appeal is charged against that car, whether it belongs to the farmer or to the grain dealer. The revenues of the country will not therefore be taxed to pay for these charges, and the business in this respect will be self-sustaining. There can therefore be no objection on the score of charges.
-Suppose the inspection is so satisfactory that there are no appeals, who pays?

Well, that is why we are [DOT] asking for this board. The difficulty is that the present board is entirely too cumbersome. There are twelve men, who the hon. member for Vancouver said were Winnipeg Exchange men. They are Winnipeg Exchange men, and they are the only men who could effectively deal with the business. It would be inadvisable to appoint any man to come from outside of Winnipeg, because you would have to pay a special salary to him, and he would have to be there all the time. The only way in which the business can be conducted is to have members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange who are accustomed to dealing in grain. These men have to be got together and as they are all busy men attending to their own affairs it is hardly fair to ask them to leave their business at a time when minutes may mean thousands of dollars to them, and where it is important to sell grain at the proper time. A man may have brought 50,000 or 100,000 bushels of grain the day before and have to dispose of it within a certain time, and time means a good deal in these circumstances. Another circumstance in connection with the matter is the fact that men do not like dealing with grain that may belong perhaps to their fellow members. There may come before them samples from friends or even their own grain and they do not like the embarrassment this causes. We want an absolutely independent board that will have no interest in any one car of grain that comes before them, men who will not be permitted to deal in grain or handle it in any way privately. It will be for the board to make such charges as will render the work self-sustaining. I visited Minneapolis on different occasions and the system there worked perfectly, and we appealed to the Government years ago for the establishment of a similar board at Winnipeg. As to the location of the board the consensus of opinion favours Winnipeg. We have our own farmers1 organizations in the three western prairie provinces and they have been looking after the affairs of those provinces in all these matters, and they also have their own two companies, which are the largest initial grain handling companies in the world. The Saskatchewan company is only a few years old but it handles 25 per cent of the entire grain produced in Saskatchewan. They have been able successfully to handle their own business on a fairly favourable basis and we believe that we have men who understand the grain business as thoroughly as those in any of the other companies. I have no particular 
interest in Winnipeg, except that we have commission officers in Winnipeg and have our terminal elevator. I am not speaking on behalf of Winnipeg, or Fort William, or Port Arthur. We have far more interest in Port Arthur than anywhere else, we have a million dollars there where we have not ten in Winnipeg in so far as real estate is concerned. If we were considering our interests in so far as property is concerned We should speak of Fort William or Port Arthur, where we have our investments. But we are not looking at it in that way. We have studied the system throughout and have considered the system in Minneapolis as well and we have come to this conclusion, without a dissenting voice, we also claim that the men who produce the article which is going to be inspected, and who pay for the charges should at least have some say as to where the operation shall take place. Primarily they are the only people interested and it is only reasonable that they should study their own interests and make recommendations as to where the board should be located. The managers of our companies who are not shareholders, at least so far as the Saskatchewan company is concerned, have no hesitation in saying that the board should be at Winnipeg where all the inspection is done. We are given to understand that sample markets will be established in Winnipeg and that being the case, samples will be taken outside of Winnipeg, just as is done in Minneapolis. Samples will be forwarded to Winnipeg by express in most cases, and the inspection can be done; and in case it is necessary to resample, if it cannot be caught at Winnipeg it can be caught at Fort William. There is an erroneous impression that where an appeal is called for it is necessary to resample the car. That is not the case. It simply means a disagreement with the man who has inspected that particular sample of grain, and the sample will go to the Board of Appeal,
In Minneapolis could not the farmer ask for a re-isample, and-is that not what you advocate in Canada?

Any farmer can ask for a re-sample of a car if he wishes, but that-has not been the case very often in Minneapolis, where they have two sampling bureaus. They have one which is maintained by the government and one by the trade itself, and they check up one with the other. We are asking now for duplicate sampling at Winnipeg to obviate as much as possible the re-sampling of cars. Altogether,

we are perfectly satisfied in our own minds that Winnipeg is the logical place for the Board of Appeals to be constituted.
I do not think I need touch upon that any farther because I think it should be patent to every one that the producers of the grain who furnish everything in connection with the elevators should at least have their interests considered. There is one other point in connection with overages that I want to touch upon. The committee wants to bear in mind that the terminal operators have absolutely nothing to do, one way or the other, with the weighing of the grain. The Dominion 'Government weigh the grain into the elevators, weigh the grain out of the elevators, inspect the grain into the elevators and inspect the grain out of the elevators. The terminal operator has absolutely no responsibility as to the weighing or grading of the grain. If the Government do not take sufficient dockage on the grain, it is their fault and not that of the terminal operator. He has to go by instructions laid down by the Government both as to grade and dockage. There might be the inference that probably the Government are not careful enough in their weighing. I would not make that assertion at all because I think the Government are as careful as they e<m be and I do not hesitate to say that it would be absolutely impossible to bring an elevator out even. In an operation covering 300 elevators, we have never yet been able to bring an elevator out even. We will have one with a big overage and another, a few miles away, with just as big a shortage.
The hon. gentleman said that he understood that these operators were paid a bonus according to their overage. I hate to take up the time of the committee but I hate to let that go unchallenged. It is only in connection with our country elevators that this bonus is allowed. We have not been operating our terminals long enough to establish a precedent or to form a basis for future action because we only got this system in operation last season and it has been in existence for too short a time to enable us to come to a definite conclusion. This season we will be in an entirely different position. With regard to the bonus we have established there are five or six different points that count favourably or unfavourably to the operator. Accuracy of weight is one and that is the only point that I shall deal with. Accuracy of weight counts twenty points. If a man has got 100 bushels of an overage and another man has got 100 bushels of a shortage, they are both dealt with exactly in the same way
in so far as the amount of the bonus is concerned. The man who gets 100 bushels of an overage does not gain one iota on the man who is 100 bushels short. I might say that we have discharged men for having large overages. While we have not discharged one for shortage where we have discharged two for overages. That is not the basis we adopt. We adopt the basis of actual, square dealing. The same thing applies exactly to the grading of the grain; we desire to secure accuracy in grading. The man who gains grades does not gain one cent by way of bonus over the man who loses grades. They are dealt with in exactly the same way on principle so that in so far as our country elevators are concerned the statement of the bon. gentleman is absolutely erroneous. That is not the basis that we follow at all.
What do you bonus them for?

That is a question that we may differ upon. We thought it would be a good thing to bonus these men to promote' efficiency. We bonus them for efficiency and what we base our bonus on principally is accuracy. The number of complaints from individuals that an operator is doing business with would be one of the things that would be taken into consideration. Another point is the giving of satisfaction generally to the community as a whole but the whole thing hinges on efficiency all the way through and no man gains on account of gaining on his grades or having overages. The man who gains on his grades or has overages is dealt with exactly the same as the man who has a shortage or the man who loses grades.
I do not think I had better take up any more time in dealing with that point; I think it has been fairly well covered. But there is one other point. One hon. member used the expression "in the interest of the public." I do not know what he meant, the public who are interested directly in the operation of these elevators are the producers of the grain. If a large overage is taken, it is just that much taken from the producers of the grain. They are the people who are directly interested in it. I do not think a fraction of one per cent per bushel would affect the consumer very much and, while I am on that point, I may say for the benefit of the minister, that I fully agree with him in fixing the amount of the overage that the elevators shall retain. I would go a little further and adopt the recommendation of our company, which is one of the largest handling companies, that the over-

age be not more than one quarter of one per cent. We originated these companies to regulate the grain business. Because the company of the hon. member for Marquette made large profits, that is nothing for which you can censure them or us. They are in that business and if they did not take the grain out of the screenings and get all they could out of it, for their shareholders, they would be derelict in their duty. They would not have done their duty if they had done differently. That is where a large per cent of your overages come from. If the hon. gentleman had gone to the trouble of looking up the returns of the Canadian Pacific elevators, where they do not reclean their screenings, he would have found that they have no overages. Am I right in that?
In one year they had a very large shortage.

In the case of the Canadian Pacific, where they do not scalp their screenings; os they call it, they have had a shortage and in no year have they had very much of an overage. The fact that the Grain Growers' Grain Company produced an overage is something for which they surely could not be condemned, because they were in it for their shareholders, whose business it is they are largely occupied in doing, and which they were in duty bound to do. They recleaned their screenings and that is where their overages largely come from. If you want to turn your screenings over to other companies with a certain percentage of the farmer's grain in it, those other companies will get the advantage of it. By the way, most of the companies mentioned by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) were not public terminal elevator companies at all.

I did not deal with the elevator companies.
Mr. MAHARG; But you read communications from some of the elevator companies.
Mr. (MANION: Yes, I beg your pardon; I thought you were speaking of overages.

I think I am correct in stating that two out of three of these companies are not public terminal elevator companies, that they are conducting private terminal elevators and it is impossible to know if private terminal elevators have an overage, as they are not asked to register.

I did not discuss the overage question at all. I was speaking of the Appeal Board and presenting the argument

of the elevators that the Appeal Board should be at the head of the lakes.

Quite so. But I want to make it clear that these are private elevator concerns that you quoted from except one. Now, I want to go a little bit farther and point out that even if you are only going to allow them one-quarter of one per cent you will not accomplish your end there for the reason that 'that one-quarter of one per cent will not exist.
I know just about what the elevator companies will do. If they get $19, $20, $25 or $30 a ton for screenings, they are not going to go to the trouble to scalp those screenings to get the grain out of it in order to turn it over to the public funds. Make no mistake about that; they can control it on the inside so that when it comes to fixing one-quarter of one per cent the Government will not accomplish what it expects to.

This is a question on which I want to get some information. I am not sure whether I understood my hon. friend to argue that the only people interested in the overages were the producers. Is that right?
Yes, they are primarily the people interested in the overages.

Well, suppose that an elevator takes in-100,000 bushels of wheat and ships it east to a flour mill in Ontario and the flour mill is 5,000 bushels short. Is that in the interest of the producer or the miller?

As I said a minute ago the Government weighs the wheat in and *weighs it out. The operator of the elevator has nothing at all to do with the weighing in or weighing out of the wheat-or the grading of it. That is a government matter purely and simply. They have their men there all the time and there is no scale that is allowed to be dumped without their inspectors seeing it.
I knorw that, but who is interested in the ishortage, the producer or the miller?

The terminal elevator will have to make up that shortage. As the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said, in the case of every car of grain that goes into the elevator a warehouse receipt is issued for the number of bushels according to the grade the inspector says they shall be, and if the terminal elevator operator at the end of the season has

not sufficient grain to fully meet the requirements of these certificates, then he has got to go on the market and purchase grain to make up the shortage. So that in the case spoken of the elevator man would be the one to make good the 5,000 bushels shortage.

If this Bill has done nothing else, in my opinion it has shown the great necessity for some new method of handling the grain trade. The hon. member for Maple-Creek (Mr. Maharg) took occasion to say before concluding his remarks that this was largely a matter of interest to those directly connected with the grain trade. I am not interested except as a citizen of Canada, and I have been rather painfully struck with the disclosures which have been made here to-day in regard to the handling of the grain as it affects the farmer or the producer. The hon member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has given figures extending over a series of years, taken from official documents, and has made the point that out of the farmers of the West for the years he mentioned tens of millions of dollars have been, as he said, illegally taken by these elevator companies and grain growers elevator companies-, which have been defended here so warmly to-day by the members for Maple Creek (Mr. iMaharg) and Marquette (Mr. Crerar). I was very much struck with the fact that although both these members have sidestepped as to the gravamen of the charge made by the hon. gentleman from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) neither of them have attempted to deny the figures that he placed upon the records- of this House, or the charge that by 'the principle upon which these elevators operate in dealing with the farmers millions of dollars which 5 p.m. belong to the farmer have been taken from him. I think it was a case where, if possible, a good defence ought to have been made in the interests of the members of this House who are connected with elevators or elevator companies, but so far the impression created by the hon. member for Vancouver is still on my mind. What I deduce from the debate is that the farmers, after three per cent of their screenings is taken from them, get the rest back. I asked the hon. member for Marquette if it were so why they -did not get the wheat back. It appears they give the farmer back the refuse but they do not give him the solid stuff; and thus tens of millions of dollars are gathered up and gar-251
nered in by the elevator companies at the expense of the farmers who sell grain to them.

The gentleman is -quite wrong in the position he is taking. With respect to the surplus screenings over three per cent there is a definite return made to the farmer for the value they can be sold at in the open market. The screenings under three per cent are taken in lieu of a cleaning charge by the elevator. If the value of these screenings were returned to the farmer the elevator company would simply have to add an additional half a cent per bushel for the cleaning, of the grain.

I was proceeding to say that this peculiar fact stands out: the point was clearly made by the member for Maple Creek that if a farmer sends- a surplus of 500 bushels he gets no credit for it in the shape of good grain. Although it belongs to the farmer it is absorbed by the elevator company. That has not been explained in this House, and it seems to me that some explanation should be forthcoming. As I take it, if the farmer is short in his weight he loses. The elevator company docks him for that shortage unless it is clearly attributable to some defect in the car. If the farmer is short in his weight I am informed by one who knows that he is charged for that in some of the elevators. Whereas, if there is a surplus the elevator company gets the benefit of it. Therefore the farmer loses in both ways-; he loses when -he is short and he loses when he is long. I do not see how this can be reconciled, and it strikes me that it is time some legislation was passed to deal with this matter. I am not in favour of the Bill as I see it. I think the principle of the Bill is right, but when T see this in par. 3:
If a surplus in any grade of grain is found in excess of one-half of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain received in the elevator during the crop year, such excess surplus shall -be sold annually by the Board- of Grain Commissioners and the proceeds thereof paid to the said board. Such proceeds shall -be applied towards cost of the administration of The Canada Grain Act in such manner as the minister may determine on the approval of the Governor in Council.
I am disappointed. I am informed when Farmer A sends a carload of grain into the market through the -elevator channels it is ear-marked; the elevator operators know that it is his grain. If he is 500 bushels long by -mistake, I do not think the Government has any right to the money



as an overage in connection with the transaction. There cannot be $10,000 000 worth of overages in these grain elevators unless the operators know where it originates, especially when it is shipped in carload lots, for the wheat is ear-marked, it is tabbed, it belongs to Farmer A or to Farmer B, and I do not think that the Government or the elevator companies have any right to the over plus that is sent in through mistake.
I did expect a better defence from those interested in elevators in reply to the allegations of the member for Vancouver. It may be of no direct interest to many hon. members by reason of their not being connected with the trade; but if his allegations are true, they shock the moral conscience of every man professing to be dealing fairly and squarely. I ask those interested in the elevators: Where has that $10,000,000 gone, where are the surpluses shown in the elevators of the companies mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver, companies with profits of 211 per cent? They only paid the farmer-shareholder seven per cent. What has become of the rest? It seems to me that that question ought to be answered. Let us have statements from the hon. gentlemen, let us have the truth, so that we may see whether the high cost of living is related to the wheat taken from the farmers which the elevator companies did not pay for.

I am not interested in the surpluses or dividends of the other terminal elevator companies. In so far as we are concerned, we have not made any. We only handled a small amount through our terminal elevator last year-not enough to base any figures on.
How about the other companies that have?
I cannot speak for those other companies.
Yes, you can.

No. What I said was that our company was brought into existence as a regulator; that is the position we take. For the information of the hon. gentleman,-and probably there are present some of the older members who were in the House at the time,-but if the late Sir Richard Cartwright was here he could tell all about the fight that the farmers put up against the terminal elevators ten, twelve

or fifteen years ago. We have been scrapping those elevators from their inception. We had to fight the whole elevator interests of the North American continent, and three or four of our farmers who had never been off the land had to come here to Ottawa and scrap with them. We asked the Government to take over the entire system of terminal elevators, but the late Laurier Government could not see their way clear to do so; they thought control -by a commission would, be the proper way. We eventually induced the late Conservative Government to start a programme of Government owned elevators to regulate the other elevators.
One of the speakers on this side of the House said, "Why not let the Grain Commission perform the service that you ask this appeal board to perform?" The Grain Commissioners are not expert grain men, they are an administrative body, and I venture to say that not one of them would pose as a grader of grain.
Some hon. members appear to have been terribly shocked at what has been disclosed here to-day. I can tel-l them something that will give them a still greater shock. When Mr. C. C. Cassel came along on one occasion unexpectedly and locked up all the elevator bins, he found that several hundred thousand bushels of low grade grain had mysteriously disappeared, but Nos. 1, 2 and 3 grades sliowed a corresponding increase. That is what we have been up against all the time, and we would have been tickled to death if the Government had taken over those elevators and operated them. But we had to build our elevators in order that w'e might arrive at a proper basis for dockage, overages, screenings, and the like, and since our elevators have been in operation we have reduced the amounit of screenings reclaimed from 5 to 3 per cent. We wanted the Grain Commissioners to reduce it to 2 per -cent, but the elevator operators said, "No. If you reduce it below that you will have to give us an additional charge."
The Canadian Grain Commission fixes all the charges of the terminal elevators for elevating, cleaning, drying, or whatever it may be-all those charges are regulated by the Grain Commissioners, so -that in a measure the charges are controlled. But it is the overages where the shoe pinches, and that is what we are endeavouring to get the Government to regulate.

Can the hon. gentleman suggest any way by which the honest farm-

er can get his share of the overages that have been stored up by the elevator companies?

Yes, but I am afraid that the method of operation would be so cumbersome that there would be nothing left. The only way that could be done would be at the end of the year to take the overages in. any one elevator, keep track of the different grain that came in from the farmers to that elevator, and then rebate to them proportionately their amount of the overages.
It is usually the grain dealer's wheat that goes into the elevators?

About 50 per cent of it on the average is grain that belongs to the elevator companies; that is, grain the title of which has left the hands of the farmer either at the local elevator or on the track. So that really the grain trade owns about 50 per cent of the grain that reaches the terminal elevators.
I thought it was 85 per cent.

No. It is 85 per cent on the other side of the line. That is the way it works with our elevator company, and I imagine it would probably work similarly with the others. The hon. member for Perth North (Mr. Morphy) spoke of farmers shipping long or short. For his information, I might say that there is absolutely no such thing as a farmer being either long or short on his wheat when it goes into the elevator.
Is not that affected by the dockage that the grain man takes without consulting the farmer?

That is at the initial point. If the committee is not wearying I shall be very glad to give this information. That leads me to another point. You are referring to the grain of the farmers that may have been sold at the other end, are you?
No. I am referring to the fact that the farmer is skinned all the way along the line wherever his grain is handled.
I am inclined to agree with you that that was so until we got our own elevators. We are trying to regulate that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Are not your own companies making money?

Certainly. Nobody is trying to hide the fact that they are. What are they in business for? ' No company could carry on at all if they did not make some money. It is so elementary that it is patent to every one. But the money we do make is made out of ourselves-out of handling the grain of our own shareholders.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Do you not take other people's grain besides the grain of your shareholders?

The percentage of grain from outsiders would probably not amount to more than 5 or 10 per cent. We have in the neighbourhood of from possibly 50 to 200 shareholders at each elevator, so we have practically all the people in the country interested with us, and if we do make profits it is from our own farmer friends, we take it out of ourselves. Even when we go into commercial business we are held down so that we can only sell to our own members.
, Mr. MORPHY:	Will the hon. member
allow me another question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I must ask
the hon. gentleman to kindly address the phair.
. Mr. MAHARG: All right, Mr. Chairman. I am hurrying along as much as I can, I .want to inform hon. members and answer their questions. Your question was that *the farmer is being docked too heavily out of his grain at the initial elevator. That is the only place where he can be docked. Any grain he ships himself goes to the elevators and is inspected by the Government inspectors, so that it is only in the case of grain at the initial point that the farmer is affected. That was exactly the position the farmers were in before we came flown to Ottawa fifteen years or more ago to get the 'Canada Grain Act-probably longer than that. The Grain Combine was one of the greatest combines in existence. The farmers were absolutely at their mercy. The railway companies refused to take a bushel of grain from any source only through the elevators of the Combine. We
3364 [DOT]

had no protection. They graded the grain as they liked, they docked it as they liked, and they paid what price they liked. There twere absolutely no restrictions, and we were '(at their mercy. Consequently we came to pttawa and interviewed the right hon. the late Sir Richard Cartwright, and got what ,was then known as the Manitoba Grain (Act, and what is now known as the Canada (Grain Act. We have been working on that (Grain Act for years, but it has not reached perfection yet. We are trying to add something to it to-day, and we will have something more to add to it later, if we do not get it this season, in order that we may perfect it as nearly as possible. We will keep trying until we do.
We were entirely at the mercy of the elevator company, but now the farmer has protection under the Canada Grain Act-that is, if he understands his business and takes the necessary precautions. Under the present regulations of the Board of Grain Commissioners the elevators all have to retain samples of grain that the farmer sells to them. The elevator company has to furnish a small tin box; the farmer furnishes a lock and retains the key, and out of every load of grain that he brings in he can compel the elevator operator to extract a fair sample and puts it in this box; this may be done whether the farmer is selling the grain or simply having it stored. If the farmer, having delivered his carload of grain or whatever the quantity may be, is not satisfied with the dockage that the elevator man has taken from him, he may, if he is selling the grain to the elevator take a sample which is satisfactory to himself and to the operator of the elevator; that sample is sent by mail to the Winnipeg inspection office, and there is graded. The inspector at Winnipeg sets the dockage on that sample of grain, and that is the dockage that the elevator company has to set if they have purchased the grain from the farmer. I am not saying that the farmer never loses, but that is the machinery with which he may protect himself in every case, if he wishes to take advantage of it.

May I ask the hon. gentleman to step away from-his own company and to explain these tremendous profits of 211 per cent made by other companies? Apparently there is no one here now to defend those companies. Some hon. gentleman who might do so were here, but they have left the Chamber.

I will explain, as well
as I can, how these elevator companies

secure these overages. As I stated, the Government weighs the grain in and weighs it out, and fixes the dockage of grain that is to be taken. If they say the grain is to be cleaned to a certain grade, it must be cleaned to that grade. If there is only a small per cent of screenings in it, they are not expected to clean the grain at all. This is one way in which they could possibly come out a little ahead,; if there is only a small percentage of dirt in the grain the elevator companies are not obliged to clean it.
Does some profit come to them because they do not have to clean it?
Yes, if there is a small quantity of small wheat or other matter in that grain they might stand to gain on that account.	.
How?

Because of not having to clean the grain. If the grain showed only a small amount of dockage it is possible that there is where a fair proportion of the overage comes in.
Mr. A. K. iMACLEAN: That is a Liverpool Grain Exchange rule, not a regulation under the Canada Grain Act.

It is a rule of the inspector, who is the king so far as concerns the determination of the grade, the dockages, and the like. He is czar, so to speak, also, in regard to the moisture content of the grain.
The Government may not always hold the elevatotr people down to the letter in respect to the amount of dockage that goes out in grain. If the grade is No. 1 Northern and the board permits a certain amount of dockage over and above what really should go out, then the elevator company stands to gain. But the chief source of overage is that mentioned by the member for Marquette. The Grain Board allow thirty pounds a car on wheat for invisible shrinkage; I think the rate is the same on oats, and a little more or flax. Flax, by the way, is something that you never have an overage on. If, therefore, you handle from ten to twenty million bushels of grain and get an allowance of half a bushel on each car, ten pounds or more of this may be saved to you, here you might have from ten thousand to twenty thousand bushels, which is another source of revenue.

Another thing which contributes is what we call the scalping of the grain. The elevator people have large cleaners and when they take in 150,000, or 200,000 bushels of grain a day that grain must he cleaned up very rapidly, because in order to do business successfully the workhouse must be kept clear. More or less grain always goes over in these screenings. I have on many occasions watched this operation for hours, and I know that a little grain always goes over in the screenings. These screenings are recleaned with what they call scalping machines and the grain which goes over is thus taken out. The amount of grain that goes over may be almost unnoticeable, but out of 39,000,000 or 40,000,000 bushels of grain you may get 30,000 or 40,000 bushels and hardly see these sprinklings of grain at all as they come over. I have seen these scalpers work; they may run twenty-four hours a day for ten or twelve months, and they may bring out quite a quantity of grain. It is possible, therefore, that there is a considerable overage on that account.
There is another source of overage in respect of which no accusation of any kind can be made against the elevator people, and that is in connection with mixed grain. A car may be graded mixed grain; it may be oats with ten or twenty per cent of wheat in it. All that wheat may be cleaned out, and a certain percentage of overage will be received from this source. There are a half a dozen or more ways in which a tremendous overage can be made up when there is a big turnover. Many of the elevators turn over twenty-five or thirty million bushels.
Does the hon. gentleman attribute the making of the 211 per cent profit to overages?
The member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) dissected those profits and said, I think, that out of the handling there was something like seven per cent
A seven per cent dividend, but 211 per cent profit.

I think he said that out of the actual handling of the grain-that is, the charges received for handling-the dividend amounted to something like seven per cent; the other dividends came from overages and screenings. There has been a tremendous revenue from screenings during the last few years. Screenings have been worth as much as $30 a ton; in fact, certain
kinds of screenings are worth more than the grain itself. If you are sufficiently adept in separating yellow mustard from the grain, the yellow mustard is a more valuable product than the grain itself. I do not know where the yellow mustard goes, but I know that they pay more for it than they do for the grain; so that that is another source of revenue. If immense profits are piled up, there is a dozen sources from which these profits may come and which it is almost impossible to cut off. What we have been trying to get at is to have every operation in connection with the elevator paying for itself so that the thing will stand on its own feet. If this was the case they would not have to say: If you cut down our screenings, you will have to let us make a higher charge for handling the grain.
That is what we want to do. If it costs one-half cent to put the grain through the elevator, we want to know that, and we want to have an account of every operation of the elevator. If there are drying charges, we want to know what they cost. Our elevator is constructed as a regulator, so that w,e may know exactly the cost of handling the grain. We hope to get that from the Government elevators, but we have not been perfectly satisfied, and we have put in our own elevator and we are putting a hospital elevator alongside of it. I will give an illustration to show what it means to have one's own elevator. We were handling grain for our shippers at the terminal elevator; we had one car of wheat -sent down to us last fall, and our salesman on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange offered that car for sale. He was not satisfied with the price that he was offered for it, as he did not consider it to ibe anything like what he should have received. While we have not the machinery in our large handling elevator to handle this grain continuously, yet we took in this one particular car of grain as this was such a glaring case of unfairness, and our operator decided that he would handle this caT through our elevator, which was not built for that purpose, but which by working slowly and interfering with our other work, could handle it. To put the matter short, the net difference between the price offered for that oar and the price received for it, after we had separated and sorted it for that farmer, was a litle over $600. One can readily understand, therefore, why I say that we are constructing this elevatoT as a regulator.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia) moved the second reading of Bill No. 137, to amend the Militia Act.

Explain.
Major-General MEWBURN: One of the amendments is in connection with section 24 of the Militia Act which reads:
There shall continue to he a permanent force which shall consist of such permanently embodied corps', not exceeding five thousand men, enrolled for continuous service, as are, from time to time, authorized by the Governor in Council.
The proposed amendment is that the word "five" be struck out and the word "ten" be substituted therefor, so as to provide that the permanent force shall consist of such permanently embodied corps, not exceeding 10,000, as are, from time to time, authorized by the Governor in Council. The permanent corps t-o-day consists of an establishment of 5,000 of all ranks, and it has been felt that authority should be granted to increase that force as circumstances may require. It is noit the intention to increase up to that number at present, but it may be necessary in the near future to add to the present permanent force in a reasonable way as may be deemed necessary.

What does the minister call a reasonable way?
Major-General MEWBURN: I should say in the neighbourhood! of 7,000 men at present. I do not know that it may not possibly be advisable to add to the force a small flying corps. At the same time, fit is not considered advisable to embody permanently a flying corps of any size. Probably one squadron would be sufficient, which could be utilized for defensive purposes if required, and which would be very valuable in connection with some of our commercial industries. It has also been considered advisable, in fact, I have recommended that one cavalry regiment be

added to the two that exist at present, namely, the Royal Canadian Dragoons and the Stratheona Horse. I would strongly urge and recommend the addition of another cavalry regiment, the Fort Garry Horse at Winnipeg. It may be considered advisable to add one infantry battalion to the permanent force, but as yet no definite decision has been reached. This leaves it to the Governor in Council to determine as to increasing the force up to 10,000, if required, and I would not urge it at present unless an emergency arose.
, Another amendment is in connection with section 53, subsection 2 which provides that fhe Governor in Council may, from time to time, fix the sums to be paid to privates in the permanent corps, having regard to .length of service, good conduct and efficiency. but the ordinary pay shall not exceed the amounts following, that is to say:

Major-General MEWBURN:	I think it
will 'be absolutely /necessary to have U small force in every military district in Canada, the infantry being distributed pro rata amongst the military districts, together with the *mounted units and the artillery. At the present time there are the Royal Canadian .Dragoons, Lord Strathcona's Horse, Royal Canadian Horse Artillery, Royal Canadian Garrison Artillery, Royal Canadian Engineers, The Royal Canadian Regiment, and the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, which has been added to it, Canadian Permanent Army Service Corps, Canadian Permanent Army .Medical Corps, Canadian Permanent Ordnance Corps, Canadian Permanent Army Veterinary Corps, Canadian Permanent Army Pay Corps, making up an establishment of 5,000.
