Mr. ANDREW R. McMASTER (Brome): Earlier in the session when the Estimates of the Militia Department were before the House I took the opportunity to congratulate the minister upon his refusal to adopt any scheme for a permanent military establishment in Canada until the peace situation had cleared up. My disappointment therefore is very great when I see to-day that we are celebrating the imminent signing of peace by proposing to pass an Act increasing by 100 per cent the permanent land military forces of this country. It does seem to me that this matter might have been left in abeyance until we and the rest of the world could see what hope of peace and disarmament the situation holds out to humanity. The great enemy who for half a century has threatened European civilization has declared his impotence by signing a peace imposing severe and drastic conditions upon him. Under these circumstances, is it wise, is it reasonable, (when the country is overwhelmed' with debt as it is, to increase the permanent forces of Canada? I do not believe it is. I had hoped that my country, after the splendid record which it established
overseas in fighting, would be in the forefront of disarmament and progress towards peace. Why should we increase our military forces by 100 per cent? The war is over; peace is to be signed, and there is no necessity for this action. When we had a small permanent force we were able, through the courage and enthusiasm of the manhood of this country, to raise an army of nearly a half million men, and if war does threaten us again, which God forbid, surely we can rely on the same admirable qualities and heroic attributes in our race as we did before. As regards the raising of pay, I think that is only proper; but I do wish to express my profound disappointment at the step which the minister is about to take. If it is not too late I would ask him to let this matter stand for the present at least.

I was not aware that the hon. member for Brome had intended to speak on this matter, but he has so adequately expressed the very ideas that have 'been running in my mind since this Bill was introduced into the House that it becomes unnecessary for me to say very much. Before the war, I had viewed with considerable dissatisfaction, if not with some alarm, the steady increase in our military estimates, and had hoped that the time would soon arrive when there would be a stay in them. Unfortunately the war broke out and our military estimates went forward by leaps and bounds. Thousands became millions. I was* one of those who believed in the prosecution of the war, so far at least as Canada was concerned, if necessary until the last man and the last dollar, to use the popular expression, had been utilized. But I had undoubtedly hoped that when the war was over there would be a retrenchment in these military expenditures. As a member of the Pensions Committee I cannot say I view with alarm, but certainly I view with some concern, the very large amount we shall annually have to expend to meet the righteous and legitimate claims of those who have made sacrifices in the war for us, and it did come to me as a shock when the minister introduced this Bill asking for leave to increase the permanent force to
10,000	men. It is all very well to say that this merely "asks for leave" to increase the force to that number. I do not think that there are many men in this House who will come to any other conclusion than that if

this leave is obtained it will not- be very many years before ~we shall have a permanent force of 10,000 men, with all the concomitant expenditures such a force will entail. I have not that full information that I should like to have to enable me to reach an unshakable conclusion, but from what I understand at the present time I do not view sympathetically the request of the minister as contained in this Bill. The League of Nations is held out to us as an institution that will prevent wars in the future. It is quite true that by section 12, I think, of the Covenant-if it is to be incorporated in the peace terms we must necessarily adopt its principles

we shall assume certain responsibilities with the rest of the world. But if this war has demonstrated one thing more than- another, it has clearly demonstrated the fact that the hero is to be found practically under every jacket, and that when there is a national crisis men may always be called upon to respond in defence of the ideals they hold and in defence of their native land. This war has not been won by the permanent forces of the world. It has been won to a very great extent by the volunteer forces of the British Empire, and it seems to me wholly unnecessary that at this- time, with the burden of debt that we are going to be called upon to assume, and in view of the urgent necessity that exists for the best efforts of every available man to increase production, we should take from the national life 5,000 able-bodied men and impose on the country the burden of maintaining a possible permanent force of 10,000. I iquite agree with the	minister-and	when
the Bill gets into Committee I intend to direct a few remarks to that aspect of the subject-that something better must be done for the permanent force whatever its size. But I cannot allow this opportunity to pass without expressing my deep regret that the Government found it necessary to introduce this Bill asking for leave to increase the permaneent force to 10,000.

I desire very briefly to associate myself with the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) in protesting against this increase in our military forces at this time. Only last week we read in the public press that the United States Congress had rejected a similar proposition of the Secretary for War and reduced his estimates for the permanent forces by one-half. In view of
[Mr. Nickle. [
this, surely it ill becomes us in Canada to increase our permanent forces by 100 per cent. I have no objection whatever to-passing what estimates the minister requires for voluntary training, but I do object at this time to doubling up our permanent military forces.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Steele in the Chair.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I quite appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Brome and I certainly was quite clear in the statement I made when the Estimates were up. I have no great desire to increase the forces but circumstances have arisen throughout the whole country which seem to indicate an absolute necessity that Canada should have some force available for the preservation of law and order in this country.
Provision is made for 10,000 men, but the force that we propose to have immediately is a relatively very small number when you consider the length and breadth of the Dominion of -Canada. It is not the intention of the -Government to increase the force at the present time to anything like the maximum number to be provided for. I do not think the- force is increased at the present time any more than is- absolutely necessary and probably by not more than a couple of thousand all told. I am as anxious as any hon. member to keep down the expenditure, and I think my conduct has proven that that is my desire. If the signing of the Peace Treaty were going to bring peace and good will all over the world we would all be delighted. -In the United States, although I -am quite aware that there was an attempt to reduce the expenditure, there were people who thought they should havq a permanent standing army of 500,000 . The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) says that the permanent force did- not win this war, but I would- like to know what he would say in regard to the " contemptible " little British army that took the field in the early stages- of the war in 1914. If it had not been for the. permanent force of Great Britain I do not know but that the results of the war might have -been different. In addition to that, a permanent force is absolutely necessary for the preservation of law and order in every country. I regret to have to say that I am confirmed in that belief by events that have been happening all over the world-; the troubles arising to the south of us and the troubles that are arising in

different parts of Canada. Judging by many letters I have had from all parts of Canada, it would appear as. if in some cases people are getting stampeded. I have even been told that the Government are negligent in that they have not a permanent standing army of at least 100,000 men in Canada. I received a letter from Winnipeg urging that the Government should have a permanent force that can deal with the situation there. The stand I take in connection with all these troubles is, I think, the right one. The militia is not organized at the present time, and we hope to get it rehabilitated. A committee is working now with the idea of incorporating into the militia members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and I am not now speaking of the permanent corps. I take the stand that in any municipality where there is trouble and where the militia have to be called out in aid of the civil power for the preservation of law and order, every citizen of Canada has the duty to perform to the State and he should link up with .the militia and do his duty. I explained to the House what took place in Winnipeg, how the militia units were filled up by the good citizens of Winnipeg commanded by commissioned and non-commissioned officers, all being enrolled temporarily for the emergency. The same thing has taken place in other parts of Canada in the west, at Toronto, Hamilton and different points.
I do not feel pessimistic about the future but I think that without any doubt I would be negligent in my duty as Minister of Militia if I did not propose that we should have some force that would be available for the preservation of law and order in the country. Taking into consideration the great extent of territory of Canada, I do not think it is an unreasonable request to ask Parliament for a mandate to increase the force to 10,000 and leave it to the Governor in Council to determine as to when that force should be increased.

I understand that before the war we had a small permanent force and that law and order throughout the country were well preserved. Now we have over 300 000 well trained men ready to take their place in the ranks at any time in defence of their country. I do not see that the country should be asked to pay for a larger force than that which we had before the war.

I would suppose in this case that the pay and expenses in connection with these 10,000 men would have to be voted by Parliament before the force was raised; consequently, Parliament at all times has in its control the poweT to regulate the number of men in this permanent force. We are, this session, voting a certain amount for a permanent force which has nothing to do with the war appropriation. The minister can only engage a sufficient number of units to use up that money and before he can increase the force he must again ask for a grant and for the consent of Parliament; he cannot go beyond the number of men for which Parliament grants the money. By this legislation the maximum will be fixed at 10,000 men, but Parliament year after year has to ratify every act of the Government in connection therewith.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of attention to what the minister has said and I have noted his explanation that this increase of 100 per cent to our permanent force is due not to apprehension of outside danger but to the fear of domestic trouble. To my mind that is a sad explanation. What the minister has said shows the intention of the department. I say to this House that force is no remedy; that it is not necessary that the Canadian people should be overawed by an increase of 100 per cent in our military establishment. As was pointed out by my hon. friend from Restigouche (Mr. Michaud) we have hundreds of thousands of men who have shown their loyalty to Canada, trained soldiers, to-day in the country. Therefore, I say that this increase in the permanent force is not necessary. Is it the fact that the minister thinks that he cannot depend on these men? Surely not. I say to the minister, as I say to this Government: Trust the people; the heart of the Canadian people is as sound as our No. 1 Hard Manitoba wheat. There is no necessity for this. If there is unrest and discontent in the country, an attempt to overawe the discontented by a 100 per cent increase in our military establishment is decidedly not the proper procedure. Trust the people I say to the Government. I would urge upon them what I have already urged from my seat in this House-summon the leaders of organized labour and the leaders of the organized employers to a joint council as has been done in the Old Country. Do not wave the red flag in the face of these discontented people by in-

creasing by 100 per cent your military establishment and telling them that we need
10,000	men to keep order in Canada. When the Northwest Mounted Police was only 600 strong it kept order in the country half the size of Europe. It is not the size of your military establishment, it is not the number of your soldiers; it is the ready obedience which the people give to constituted authority that is necessary.
I would ask the minister to reconsider this matter and if he is not prepared to do *so I will take it upon myself to move the rejection of section 1. I therefore move the rejection of the clause.
. The CHAIRMAN: A motion for the rejection of the clause would not be in order. There is already a motion before the committee that the clause do carry. The hon. gentleman can vote against it.
. Mr. McMASTER: I will express my view by voting against the clause.
. Mr. MORPHY:	I apprehend that the
minister in putting forward this Bill has good reasons for so doing. The fact that he has stated .that from the West and other parts of Canada the requests which have come to him have led him to put forward the Bill is a factor that should be considered. The country is large and the number of men in proportion to the extent of the country is small. If one could rely on the opinion expressed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Niclde) that with the League of Nations war would be at an end, there might be some reason for considering the necessity of the force contemplated by the minister, but in my opinion the League of Nations is too young yet for any country in the world to bank upon its efficacy to prevent war. There might be to-morrow or the day after a sudden upheaval which would throw the world again into war. The hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Michaud) says that we have 100,000 men who have come through the war, but I do not think it is a very charitable proposal that we should send these men back again immediately to fight the battles of the country, whether domestic or foreign. The League of Nations is having its own troubles. We realize every day that Japan is uneasy, that there may be an attack on the integrity of 'China, that Korea is in a condition of unrest and that a conflict may break out any day. Surely we must all reflect upon the condition of things that existed before the last war. Men derided the iSea that there would be a war and it
[Mr. .MfoMaster.l
was scoffed and laughed at in many quarters; it was not taken seriously. At this time I rather resent the attitude of the hon. member for Brorne (Mr. McMaster) who, I think, descended just a little below his usual level when he uttered the sentiments to which he gave expression. It seemed to me to be something like pandering to politics, pandering to the w'orking classes of the country and inciting the workingman, in so far as he could do it, against the organized, executive force of the government of the country. It seemed to me that he uttered a plain invitation or incitement to the disruption of the country's affairs. Goodness knows that the unrest to-day in Canada is not necessarily a sufficient warrant for the Bill that is before the House, but it is a factor, and I do not think it is fair for the hon. member for Brome to rely upon the statement which he does rely upon that this force is for that specific purpose. The minister does not put it forward in that way, and I do not think it is fair that any member of the House should so represent it. Canada is populated by a very widely diversified people. We have sections on the Pacific Coast, on the Atlantic coast, and all over, where a force may be necessary any moment to defend the best interests of the country. Belgium with her small force of 170,000 at the beginning of the war kept the Germans back for eighteen days and helped to win the war. We must not denude ourselves of a military force in this country. When the League of Nations is formed and peace is settled and the day comes when this force can be otherwise utilized or done away with, then will be the time to take action to that end.

speechtext:
When the Committee
rose at six o'clock clause 1 was under consideration. Shall clause 1 carry?

Before clause 1 is voted
on, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two in reply to the Minister of Militia's answer to my argument. If I understood him correctly, he endeavoured to argue that because Great Britain sent an expeditionary force of 100,000 men to Prance, therefore there was justification for Canada having a permanent force of 10,000 men. In 1914 the British Expeditionary Force was probably the finest-trained and best-equipped force in the world, and without doubt the part it played in the early stages of the war was most important in giving the Allies an opportunity of preparing for the subsequent warfare. But I fail to follow the logic of the minister in his argument,-if that was his endeavour-that because Great Britain maintained a permanent army of 100,000 men before the great war, that is a justification for Canada hereafter having a permanent force of 10,000 men. Great Britain has for more than a century been the policeman of the world. She has colonies in all parts of the world and protectorates in the Seven Seas. England to a great extent, if not altogether, finds it essential for the maintenance of the British Empire that there should be available at all times a disciplined force that can be sent, as occasion may require, to any part of the world.
I do not believe that the time has arrived when Canada, as a part of the British Empire, feels it incumbent to assume any part of the policing of the world, except in so far as our obligations under the Treaty of Peace, which embraces the League of Nations, may necessitate such duty. I am quite prepared to admit that probably by being a signatory to the Treaty of Peace Canada will assume obligations that will place her among the nations of the world-obligations that may, in time to come, necessitate our sending troops to any part of the world for the maintenance of the status* quo of things in general. But I have greater hopes for the League of Nations than that we are immediately going to be required to maintain peace by the use of arms. There is no great mystical power in the term "League of Nations,"
and probably the covenant between the signatories to the Peace Treaty will, to a very great extent, depend for its true fulfilment upon the spirit in which it is entered into and the spirit manifested in the keeping of that League.
But I want again to reiterate what I said to the House this afternoon, that with the financial obligations Canada has to face in the near future, I do not think this is the time for us to assume what would probably be an obligation of 17,500,000 for years to come. If we add 5,000 men to our permanent force, at $1,000 per man for maintenance, that will represent $5,000,000 a year, and by the time you add to that the equipment and the additional remuneration that must be paid to the higher rank's, to say nothing of the other expenses incident to such an organization, I do not think I am outside the figure when I say that Canada's bill for the maintenance of her permanent force will amount, not to $7,500,000, but to $15,000,000 a year. For these reasons, Mr. Chairman, I am against the power that is asked for. I regret exceedingly that the minister has brought in the Bill, and as>
I am now inclined. I am sorry to say, I cannot support it.
Major-General MEWBURN: In reply to the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), what made me refer to the permanent corps was that in his remarks the hon. gentleman, I think I am correct in saying, made the statement that the permanent forces did not win the war. I quite concur in that, but I do say that if it had not been for the standing or permanent army of Great Britain in 1914, which held the line between Mons and the Marne, I do not know where we would have been; and I think everybody will admit that in the early stages of the war the small permanent corps of Canada, which were called out immediately, made a record for themselves that will never be forgotten. That is* what I had reference to as far as the permanent corps is concerned, I do not agree with my hon. friend's remarks as regards, the necessity of having the permanent corps increased. All I am asking in this Bill is to give power to the Governor in Council to increase the permanent corps to such number, not exceeding 10,000 men, as they may determine. The hon. member well knows that the permanent corps cannot be increased until proper Estimates have been brought down and passed1 for their allowance and upkeep. But I do not think Canada to-day can

afford to be without a trained force of moderate * size to meet any eventualities that may occur. I am a great believer in the maxim that it is Ibetter to foe sure than sorry, and I think it is very poor policy to be penny wise and pound foolish. I felt it incumbent upon me to advise the Government that the permanent force should be increased in a small way, but at the present time not up to 10,000 men. I think, however, there should he provision in the statute that the force may be increased up to that point if the necessity arises. I think I have explained all the other matters referred to foy my hon. friend, and I do not feel "it necessary to continue the argument.

I would just like to point out in connection with this Bill an experience I had when in Winnipeg about ten days ago. I had an interview with General Ketchen, who is in charge o<f Military District No. 10, as to the troubles in Winnipeg. I asked him in reference to the military strength that might foe available there should the conditions prove more serious. I discussed the matter with him and suggested that inasmuch as there were thousands of demobilized troops he would have no difficulty in securing all the men he might require. On the contrary, he said, he had extreme difficulty, that these men did not manifest any willingness to organize again,-they had been demobilized, were sick of the job, and did not wish to participate in military service again immediately. As a result an appeal was made to the citizens of Winnipeg, and some thousands of the business men organized and were sworn in to the militia. They repaired to the various barracks and went through the necessary drills, and performed all manner of menial work, during which time, they were, df course, obliged to absent themselves from business. I am prompted to make these remarks' because of a statement by one of the hon. members on the other side of the House that we had a very large militia force in the country which would always foe available.
I join with the hon. gentleman in paying tribute to the fine character of these men, and I concur in his remark about the stability of the Canadian people. But we are facing a condition, not a theory, and in view of the experience that the people of Winnipeg have had within the last few weeks, and of the advisability of providing for the taking of proper steps should
[Major-General Mewburn.]
similar incidents occur in any other part of the country, I am a strong believer in the idea that there ought to be a permanent force. The minister does not propose that the permanent force shall consist of 10,000 men; the Government is simply being given power to have a permanent force up to that number. I think that is only fair. The Government is charged with the responsibility of protecting the people and of preserving peace throughout the country. Our country is three or four thousand miles long, and if trouble should break out in two or three places at the same time the Government would be blamed, and properly so, if it had not taken precautions to deal with such a situation. After what has been said, I have no doubt that the Government will certainly not increase the force beyond what is reasonably necessary. Hon. members should bear in mind the heterogeneous nature of the population in the far western country, especially in British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan. Hundreds of thousands of these people do not understand our constitution, many thousands of them are not even familiar with our language; and until they are assimilated with our own people it would be wise to have a very considerable permanent force. Until the present unrest subsides-and it exists throughout the country to a much greater extent than members who have net been in t.heir constituencies lately would dream of-the Government should be on the alert to meet any possible emergency that may arise.
Mr. CRERiAR: I cannot quite agree with the views expressed by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Richardson); nor am I by any means convinced of the wisdom of increasing our permanent military establishment by 100 per cent. If we look at the matter from the point of view of establishing the basis of a military organization to meet such an emergency as this country was called upon to meet in 1914, what we accomplished at that time clearly shows that we do not need any addition to the forces now. In other words, with a permanent force of
5,000	prior	to	1914, we	had the
skeleton of an organization upon which, in a short time, we built up an army of 500,000-and the most efficient army that was engaged in the great war. Consequently, it does not appeal to me as necessary that for this purpose we should make provision to enlarge our permanent military establishment.

The only other consideration that qould lead ns to view favourably the suggestion contained in this Bill is the maintenance of law and order at home. I have faith in the law-abiding qualities of the Canadian people; I dislike even to contemplate an increase in the permanent military establishment to 10,(100 with a view to maintaining law and order in this country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Richardson) has stated that the citizens of Winnipeg, where there has been grave unrest for the past six or seven weeks, took upon themselves the obligation of maintaining law and order there. If it should be necessary in other parts of the country-all hon. gentlemen, I am sure, devoutly hope that it will not-to maintain law and order, the same means could be found as have been found in Winnipeg. I am profoundly convinced that the maintenance of law and order and the bringing of happiness to the people lies not so much in creating armed forces as it does in en-4gavouring to strike at the causes which lead to unrest. The creation of this force will mean an additional annual outlay, as the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has pointed out, of from $5,000,000 to $7,500,000 a year. Having regard to the present state of our finances and to the revenue which this country has to raise, is it desirable to undertake the additional expenditure involved in this proposal ? It does not commend itself to my judgment. I hope that the Government will direct all the attention it possibly can to removing the causes of the unrest which exists in the country today ; that is the best possible remedy for present conditions and the most efficacious means of bringing back harmony and happiness to the Canadian people. I believe that the vast majority of the foreign element of our population-and by this I mean the elements in our population which are of European foreign	extraction-are	lawabiding. I doubt if any country in the world with so large a percentage of alien population has come through the war as successfully, from the point of view of the absence of internal disorder, as Canada has. That being the case, let us appeal to the good. that is in our citizens rather than to the establishment of large armed forces to overawe them.

I congratulate the minister on the step that he has taken. I cannot agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Crerar), for I know of no country which has so much to defend and so little to defend it as Canada has. Suppose we had a
permanent force of 10,000 for the whole of Canada; that would be two and a half men for every mile of our four thousand miles of border. Surely an army of such a size and so disposed would not be very successful in the trenches against an ordinary enemy. But while we are not contemplating any trouble of that kind, it is only a matter of ordinary precaution that we should take out a certain amount of insurance in this connection-for I look upon this provision as a kind of insurance policy, and a very moderate one, indeed. Had the minister proposed the stablishment of a permanent force up to 25,000 men, a great many people would have held up both hands for it. Ten thousand men is the very minimum for a permanent force in this country. I do not know what our responsibilities will be under the League of Nations. Force will be used if the League of Nations is to amount to anything; even the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) will admit that. The League of Nations is not going to bring about peace in the world simply by a fiat. It has not been able to do away with the trouble in Russia, though representatives of twenty or thirty of the nations of the world are assembled over there and are controlling many millions of men. Notwithstanding all this, Russia is still seething with revolt, bloodshed and destruction, and what applies to Russia applies to many other European countries. Not more than six or eight weeks ago it was announced in big head-lines in the press that the United States proposed, if necessary, to establish a permanent force of 500,000 men. Our force of 10,000 as compared with the force of 500,000 men to the south would be a very limited one. indeed. I trust the Committee will sustain the minister in no uncertain way if a vote is called for on this question, because it is a matter of serious consequence to the people of Canada. If, as the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has just said, there are causes for unrest in Canada, I do not think we are going to multiply them by having a kind olf respectable police force. Even Toronto "the good," has never been able to abolish its police force, and I do not believe it will in our time.
Do not reflect on Toronto, please.

There is a certain irresponsible element in the best of cities, and a police force is required. Even the

hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) will acknowledge that that is an ordinary statement of fact that cannot be gainsaid. If that be the case in the most Christian cities of the world, surely it is not too much to say that 10,090 men for the whole Dominion of Canada-and it is not proposed to increase the force to that number at the present time-will be too great a force for Canada to embark on a little later on. I trust the minister will be very heartily supported.
Does the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) know that the United States Congress rejected their war proposition?

Can the minister say what is the attitude of the United States now as regards a permanent force for that country as compared with its permanent force before the war? Can the minister also state the attitude of Great Britain in that regard?
Major-General MEWBURN: The United States Secretary of State for War, and the War Council, determined that they were to have a standing army of 500,000 men, and I am not so clear that the Bill was rejected in its entirety. The chief dispute was in connection with the air force there, and I presume that is to be cut down. I have not seen any accurate figures, but 500,000 was the estimate. For years the United States had a National Guard throughout the States. They contemplated in some way changing that National Guard, and they felt that, with their draft law as they had it on their statute book they could get men in a hurry in case of war outside of the country, but their difficulty was in providing trained officers and instructors. While there was some talk of reducing that force below the 500,000, they intended to keep a very strong standing army and to increase yery largely their personnel of officers, i As regards Great Britain, a committee has been working for some time on the post bellum army of Great Britain, and I do not think any definite decision has yet been arrived at as to' what the standing army will be, and I do not think one will be reached until after they get through with the difficulty on the continent, but I understand it will be considerably increased.
i Mr. EDWARDS:	Has the minister the
[DOT]figures of the United States permanent army before'the war? tlMr. Cocksbutt. 1
Major-General MEWBURN:	Possibly a
little over 100,000.

The information I have here from a New York newspaper is that the United States War Department asked for
500,000	men and Congress has cut that down to 300,000.

The minister's proposition has my hearty endorsement. *When a minister comes to this House at a time like this and asks for the privilege of fortifying himself, the least this House can do is to give him that privilege. I do not think we should ask the men who have come back to Canada after four years at the front, to go out and risk their lives again in defence of this country unless we are going to pay them adequately. There is something coming to those men. Many of them came back without any occupation to return to and many of them would like to enter military life as a profession. This country owes them something, and it. can pay part of that by enlarging the permanent corps and giving a number of returned officers and men employment. We have all heard for many years past suggestions made like those of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). We know the result of them in the past; those arguments are not new, and they are as fallacious as they are old. If you want to be in a position to keep order and to enforce law in any country, you must have the necessary force. In this country, which is 4,000 miles in width, it is no use saying that you are going to enforce, law and order unless you have something behind you. The minister is to be congratulated in bringing down this-Bill, and the Committee should support him.

This is a very serious matter. I find myself very much embarrassed by it. I am embarrassed on grounds of my relationship with and my opinion of the minister. I hold the opinion that he has been a most excellent minister and that he has brought to the discharge of his duties a combination of energy and courtesy which have been a very great national possession in the very serious time through which we have recently passed. I feel that so much that I am almost sure he would not have proposed this, however strongly he might have felt in favour of it, unless he had had very strong reasons to bear upon his mind. At the same time, the proposition is serious, and it is also somewhat peculiar.

I had occasion, at an earlier period of the day, to remind the House that I for one, defended in most unmistakable terms the Military Service Act on the ground that we were fighting militarism. There was no phrase so common on the lips of the statesmen of the Allies as the phrase "We are fighting militarism, and militarism must die." Was that all a dream? Did we not mean it? If we were fighting militarism, it seems rather a peculiar thing-
I would ask the hon. member to define the meaning of the word "militarism."

There are some things that, in the matter of definition, afford a field in which a child can baffle a philosopher. There are some' things so simple that it is impossible to define them, but if my hon. friend wants to know what I think is militarism, it is the tendency of a State to remain in that stage of human society which is characterized by warlike operations. It is the state, philosophers would tell him, which is opposed to the industrial state. [I should speak much longer than I intended to on this question, if I am to have many questions like this addressed to me. If my hon. friend had spent as much time reading Herbert Spencer as I have, he would have learned that, in the opinion of that distinguished philosopher, human society passes, in the case of any given section of it, from the stage of primitive 'barbarism through a period of militarism into a state of industrialism.
Free trade later on.

Free trade and militarism are sworn foes, and therefore, I am a sworn foe of militarism. In a state of perfect industrialism, we should, of course, have free trade. It is elementary that every country would then produce a superabundance of the things it was most calculated to produce and that the different countries would exchange their surpluses with one another.
I was saying, when I was tempted to go into this argumentative alleyway, that we fought militarism in this war. We understood that we were putting down militarism. Everybody said so. Then we fought the war under a delusion, if we are going in for militarism in this country. There is another peculiar aspect of this matter. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir
Robert Borden) has just come from the Paris conference, at which the various statesmen recognized that militarism was a bad thing. There was militarism, if it was ever seen in the world, in Germany, and the statesmen at that conference have recognized it as so bad a thing that they have taken what many people regard as tremendously severe steps to cure Germany of it. Surrounded as she is by land, her existence threatened on the land as much as ever that of Britain, an island, could be by sea, she has had her standing army reduced to almost infinitesimal proportions. Surely there is food for thought in the fact that in this democratic country of Canada, at a time when we are destroying militarism in all the old autocratic countries in Europe with the apparent consent of the peoples of those countries, we should be increasing that very thing on this continent, where under the Monroe doctrine we thought we should never have to interfere in the wars of the world, and where at one time Canada's participation in such a war as that through which we have just passed would not have been thought of by any serious-minded person?
I have not had the good fortune to listen to the whole of this debate, but I gather that the reason for which we are being asked to increase the permanent military forces by one hundred per cent has been given as the unrest that prevails in the country. Well, in regard to that unrest, I should like to say that I personally have no apologies to offer for being a Canadian, in view of what has happened in Winnipeg, for this reason: That there probably never was in the history of the world a strike of such dimensions in a limited area, in which the peace-loving instincts of the people have preserved order in a manner so creditable to a whole country. I want to say, and I think that every Canadian will agree with me, that if that strike could happily be settled in the near or immediate future, instead of giving this country a black eye. the way in which it has been conducted ana the peace kept will be the best advertisement that Canada has ever received as a country to which peace-loving men may come to live without fear of being unduly molested in the pursuit of their daily avocations. So far from the unrest being an argument for increasing the military forces, the unrest in Winnipeg is exactly the other way. We have had the most acute state of feeling as between two sections of the community there. I do not want to

go into the merits of the case, hut I say that what has happened in Winnipeg does not in any case afford very strong evidence that this is a country which needs a great body of soldiers to keep its people in order, even in times of great industrial. division and strife. Now, if there is to be a vote on this matter-I understand my hon. friend from Marquette has spoken, and I am sorry I did not hear what he said-I think I shall be almost constrained, although our party is so small on the cross benches, to vote with my leader. If anything could prevent me from doing so it would be a very firm assurance from the minister that tins is a very temporary matter. And even that assurance would not carry me very far, because militarism is like strife at the beginning, it is like the letting out of water; once you enter upon this business and if my hon. friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Greisbach) or any one else doubts this, I would recommend to him a study of Cob-den, not on free trade but on armaments -once . you enter upon this business you create an appetite for it on the part of a certain class of the community, and it grows in spite of the best intentions of governments and their individual members. I cannot think that the step is a wise one. I do not think it is needed; I do not think that it' is necessary to double the standing army in Canada; for I have supreme confidence in the common sense and sanity of the Canadian people. We have heard again and again the definition of Liberalism as "trust in the people, qualified by prudence." If that be a correct definition of Liberalism I think I am still a Liberal, and I think that prudence would take the form of keeping our standing army at its present figure. The opposite definition is that of Toryism, which I think is dead in the world to-day except for a very few specimens left in the "Unionist party. Toryism has been defined as "distrust of the people qualified by fear.'' Well, we have not much to be afraid of in a country which at a moment's notice raised four or five hundred thousand of the best soldiers that.were ever seen on the face of the earth-men who would go through anything and go anywhere. We did that almost at a moment's notice in this country, and I do think that we should cast fears to the wind and be guided by reasonable prudence. We should have in mind	the	enormous financial	demands of	the country, and	the
splendid history of Canada throughout its whole record as a peace-loving country, and should rightly consider the special

record in Winnipeg to which I have referred and the way our people have kept the peace there in spite of temptation to go the contrary road. As I have said, if this question is put to the vote I shall stay with my leader unless he votes for it.

I should like to give the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) a definition of militarism which I fancy has been prepared by lexicographers who have read Spencer, and which I think it is desirable should be more or less accepted if the discussion is going to proceed along the line which it has taken. Militarism is defined as a condition that prevails in a country which makes it the chief object of the state to prepare and wage war. If that definition of militarism is accepted it follows that Germany was given over to militarism.
But does it follow that if we raise our permanent police force from 5,000 to 10,000 men we are thereby going in for militarism to the ruin of our immortal souls? Following all great world conflicts there is necessarily a period of local and international unrest. It has always been, and I fancy it always will be, so; and while I quite agree with those who suggest that we should go to the sources of the unrest and deal with them, which I hope will be done, it is very desirable-and I think it will be a strong antidote 'to some portion of ttuT unrest-if the Government of the country is able to guarantee protection to law-abiding people. That is the position in which I would put the government of this country: That those who do obey the law and desire to be law-abiding shall be protected, at all events against those who are not law-abiding.
The permanent corps played a very important part in preparing for the last war, and it is always bound to play an important part in our military preparations. No commander in the field, no man of any rank, could have qualified as he did in the Canadian army, had it not been for the instruction he received at the hands of the permanent corps. The hon. member for Red Deer pointed out how, in a moment, we raised an army. As a matter of fact, we raised, in six weeks, 33,000 men to proceed overseas, hut six months passed before they got into the field. That fact should be known. If any hon. gentleman who is satisfied with the condition of affairs in which we stood in 1914, he is easily satisfied and he is dis-

tinetly a gentleman who did not place himself in a position to suffer for lack of preparation as some of us did. By reason of lack of training, lack of preparation, lack of equipment, lack of everything that we required, it cost this country a great deal more than it need have cost to put our army in the field. In our army, particularly in the American army, and in any army where there is no adequate preparation, the casualties must be higher. You must pay the price in life and money for your failure to make adequate provision for war which is almost inevitable. It may interest the Committee to have its attention drawn to these facts in the history of our own country. We have had a chance to go to war almost every fifteen years since this country began. There was 1914, 1900, 1885, 1870, 1866 -the Fenian raid,-1837, 1812-15, and the American Revolutionary War. Will anybody say that the history of the past will not repeat itself?
As far as the city of Winnipeg is concerned, the people of that city have conducted themselves in a highly creditable manner, but it ought not to be forgotten that it is probably, to some extent, due, in addition to the splendid character of the Canadian people, to the facf that there were under arms in that city a thousand cavalry and several thousand infantry. That seems to me to afford a somewhat better explanation of the good order that has been maintained in the city of Winnipeg than to say that it is due to the kindly disposition of the people of Winnipeg, excellent people as they are. I shall support this Bill.
. Mr. D'ANJOU (Rimouski) (translation): Mr. Chairman, before the vote is taken, I think it is my duty to express my opinion upon this Bill.
I represent a county which is known for its anti-militarist principles, I am myself an out-and-out anti-militarist and I must immediately .state that it is with the greatest pleasure I shall vote against this Bill and that I will vote as often as the opportunity to do so is offered me. This is not the proper time to attempt introducing militarism in Canada after the Canadian people, for the past four years, being asked to go and fight overseas in order to destroy Prussian militarism; it is not the proper time to establish ,a military caste in Canada, to create positions, not for the men who have fought, probably, for young officers, who sported themselves in this country during four years, being paid at the rate of $10 per diem.
Mr. Chairman, as several members have already stated in this House, the League of Nations has 'been formed and it is almost a certainty that we shall not have any more wars in the future. Besides, according to the hon. Minister of Militia, this Bill has been introduced to increase our establishment, not for the protection of our borders, but especially to restore peace in the-country, to put down strikes and face all other troubles that might arise.
Mr. Chairman, I was anxious to declare that I am absolutely opposed to this Bill, without any reservation whatever, and that it will toe with pleasure; I repeat it, that I shall give my vote against this measure.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is a very ill-chosen time to double this country's military forces. As the member for Red Dear (Mr. Clark) has just stated, we have a perfect trust in the people and we believe that the best police we can have to maintain order among the people is their own good sense and their love of peace.
A moment ago the hon. member for Edmonton (M. Griesbach) said that an increase of the police force of the country was desired toy doubling the number-
of the militia.

Not of the militia, but of the military police. However, if the great conflict which took place, if the sacrifices the country 'made, if all the sacrifices of the allies have accomplished in order to establish and maintain democracy, to sustain liberty and set up a reign of universal peace are useless, it is also useless to say that, in a peaceful country like Canada, we shall gain anything in arming ten thousand men.
The stand taken by those who are opposing this increase for the time being is a wise one and, I think, the best means of ending the unrest now existing in the country would be to show the people that we have confidence in them. I do not think the words uttered by the hon. member for Edmonton very wise when, speaking about the Winnipeg strike and the general uneasiness caused by this large 'strike he says that if there was no .blood shed, if there was relative calm-because in such times calmness must ne considered relatively with the state of minds at the time-it is due to the fact that so many cavalrymen were ready to strike and that 9,000 men were under arms. Such



words are not calculated to bring peace or harmony to the country. We must not lead Canadian citizens to believe that if, for one reason or another, we must to-day increase the military strength, it is because we feel no confidence in their patriotism and their loyalty and because we think that they do not know how to appreciate this precious gift of sovereignty they enjoy in Canada.
Therefore, and following the wise advice handed to us by the hon. member for Red Deer we must place our confidence with the people, knowing that the mass of people are wise enough to keep peace and harmony in the country and I shall oppose the Bill doubling the military strength of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, if I speak on this question at all it is because the two last speakers have addressed the Committee in French, and I desire to have this section of the House know something about their ideas and their opinions.

speechtext: I think the point of order raised by the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is well taken. There is a rule which says that an hon. member cannot repeat either his own arguments or the arguments used by other hon. gentlemen.

Red Deer, and which was also stated, I think, much more as an idealist, by the member for Marquette. But the condition is wrong, absolutely wrong, and any one who suggests to me that there is any militarism in an enormous country extending from Cape Breton to Vancouver-
Do not say Cape Breton, now.

All right,-with a population scattered from the Maritime Provinces to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, to the Prairie Provinces and so to the province of British Columbia-that any one who suggests to me that a force of anything within the maximum which the hon. Minister of Militia has mentioned to-night savours of militarism-such a suggestion I cannot follow. To my mind it is only a force which is reasonable and adequate for our enormous territory and scattered population. We all deplore the present condition of unrest; we all feel we have to face it from day to day and overcome it; and we all believe that we can, having the force provided for by the Bill successfully deal with any emergency which may hereafter confront us. Therefore I shall vote for the Bill.

I had expected that my hon. friend from Edmonton East (Mr. Mackie) would have made strange revelations about the speech delivered by my good friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau); but after this address to the committee this evening, I have yet to learn that the hon. member for Three Rivers has uttered any words in French which he could not repeat in English. As a matter of fact, I take exactly the same attitude as my hon. friend from Three Rivers. That hon. member-
I rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Is the hon. member for Maisonneuve at liberty to repeat anything that has been said by the hon. member for Three Rivers?

I am not repeating at all. I am stating, Mr. Chairman, that I am taking exactly the same attitude on this Bill as my hon. friend from Three Rivers. To show those of the committee who do not understand French that there is nothing sinister in the language used or in the attitude taken by my hon. friend from Three Rivers, it is this: The member for Three 
Rivers, the member for Maisonneuve, and many other members on both sides of the House, trust implicitly the common sense ,pf the Canadian people. That is all that' was embodied in the remarks made by the hon. member. I have for my hon. friend the Minister of Militia the highest regard, and I think I may oppose his measure without impairing that regard.
It seems to me that in the great economic crisis which one section of the country is passing through to-day, if the Government had shown some moral courage it would have accomplished much more than has [DOT]been accomplished by the shots that were fired on the people of Winnipeg the other day. Remember, Mr. Chairman, I do not take sides with the strikers or against them;
I am not familiar with the conditions. The press has been absolutely silent on the causes of this strike and on the attitude of the strikers. But I admire the spirit of the citizens of Winnipeg who decided that law and order should be maintained, and they have to a laTge degree succeeded in accomplishing their purpose. I wish to say, however, that there are other examples in other countries of economic troubles such as those we have at Winnipeg and in other centres of our Dominion, and in those countries the heads of the Government have thought it their duty to interfere personally. Let me give an example to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister. Mr. Lloyd George, the Prime Minister of England, not more than a few weeks ago, was summoned from Paris-where the right hon. gentleman was-to attend a conference with the miners in England. On several occasions during the war, but certainly on two or three decisive occasions, Mr. Lloyd George, the Prime Minister of England, went to the strikers' homes -and discussed with them their troubles, and won his point, whilst the miners and the strikers were also winning theirs. Through conciliation, through parleying, and through mutual trust the labour troubles, which were of great magnitude, were overcome by the great moral strength of Mr. Lloyd George.
Let me give another example to the right hon. gentleman. 1 was reading last night the latest book-and it is an admirable book, the life of M. Clemenceau, "The Old Tiger"-by M. [Lecomte, one of the- leading French writers. During M. Clemenceau's first tenure of office as Premier of France there were two great strikes, involving not one city but two or three departments.

The men- were splendidly organized, and we know that Frenchmen are warm-blooded. There were some people who said, like my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach) -who served so gallantly during the war- that the only thing which would prevent trouble would be the calling out of the troops. M. Clemenceau resisted that proposal and himself went amongst the strikers and discussed with them their grievances, and settled both strikes. The writer says that it was due to his common sense, to his moral courage, and also to his great character, that on those two historic occasions he was able to curb the militaristic spirit which, even in France, was displaying itself against the labour element. I say to the right hon. gentleman,-and I say it with all due respect, because he knows that I have the highest regard for him that even to-day it is not too late for him. the first citizen of Canada, to go to Winnipeg, and by means of conciliation to settle the strike there. Let it not be said that the Parliament of Canada on this first explosion in the West has answered by doubling our militia force, when I believe that the right hon. gentleman, having the whole nation at his back, could by speaking words of truth and wisdom bring the parties together.
The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) spoke words of wisdom a moment ago when he said that you must strike at the root of the trouble; that you must not attempt to overcome these difficulties by force of arms. If the Government should to-morrow announce that they will introduce legislation providing for the nationalization of the cold storage establishments of this country, it would allay the bad feeling which prevails as against the monopolists. If the Government should to-morrow take steps to prevent some of these companies from corralling the money of the people to the extent of /2 per cent of profits on the necessaries of life, they would be taking steps to allay the bitter feelings which are spreading throughout the land. I agree with the member for Bed Deer that it is regrettable that on the eve of the signing of the Peace Treaty it should become known that Canada is acting contrary to the decisions arrived at at Versailles. This war is the last war, this war was meant to end all wars in the future; and it is not by doubling the military forces of 'Canada that you will instil into the minds of coming generations a recognition of the fact that we are a British country; that we have no love for militaristic enterprises, that the affairs of the country should be run on a common sense, busi-. ness basis.
I do not like, Mr. Chairman, certain expressions which were used by my gallant friend from West Edmonton (Mr. Griesbach). Speaking of the necessity of having a strong military force in Canada, he delved into history and said that every fifteen years we had " a chance " to go to war. I do not like that expression; it smacks of militarism. It would seem that my hon. friend is happy because this evening we are having the thin edge of the wedge-

When I said that eveTy fifteen years we had a chance of going to war, I meant that those who went to war had a chance to go to war every fifteen years. I went because I believed it to be my duty to go.

My ihon. friend did not go alone; fortunately, he came back alive. I accept his explanation, but the whole tenor of his speech indicates that he is in favour of the establishment and maintenance of a strong military force in Canada. The member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) went a little further; he said that it was the intention^ to give employment to returned soldiers. Is it good policy to give soldiers who went to war to end all wars further employment as soldiers on their return? I am in favour of a moderately strong military force in Canada; I advocated not long ago the training of our young boys at college in case of an emergency in the future. But let us not have militarism in Canada at a time when there is a general desire to cut the frills of militarism; at a time when we must do away with waste in the Militia Department. I do not say that the minister is wasting money, but I do say that, having regard to the period of unrest through which we are passing, to the huge national debt which is staring us in the face, and to the economic problems which confront us in the West, this is not the time to weld such a costly weapon. Again I ask the minister to consider this matter seriously; I ask him not to excite the prejudices of labour at this particular juncture.

Mr. Chairman, it is an old saying that after the storm generally comes a calm; so I am going to try and be calm.
I am going to support, in all fulness, the measure of the minister, on this particular

principle: that down in my country, when strikes come on, the employer and the employee are generally able to get together and settle their difficulties. So that to my part of the country this is a matter of indifference. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company and the Dominion Coal Company met with their employees in the court house in Sydney last January, talked over the questions at issue in a sane and complacent manner, . and arrived at a settlement of their difficulties. If you boisterous people in the West deserve to have a doubling^ of the military forces, Why then, we will give it to you.
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) does not. seem to be as familiar with strike conditions as he is with military conditions. You talk of the big strikes of the world; did governments intervene? Who intervened in the case of the Homestead strike in the United States, perhaps the biggest strike that ever occurred there? Did the British Government interfere in the London dock strikes? Was it not Cardinal Manning who settled the London dock strikes when your great Gladstone was in power? Now you call upon the Prime Minister to go to the West. Have we not had strikes in this country? Did the then Prime Minister, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, go to Glace Bay a few years ago to settle the strike down there? Now, be reasonable in this matter. Gladstone did not settle the London dock strikes; neither did the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier settle the big Glace Bay strike, which lasted for months. We had to come to terms ourselves, and we did it, by a sanity peculiar to our own Cape Breton people.
To-day there is no dispute between capital and labour in that part of the country. The only dispute we have, I might in a friendly way remind the Government, is that they are not getting back our shipping. If in the western country you have difficulties of your own, do you know of any statute that you people who were in charge of the affairs of this country put on the statute book that would settle such disputes? Do you know of any law that you ever put upon the statute book that would allow any of your members of Government, or officials of your departments, to go out to Winnipeg and take conditions in your own hands and settle that strike? Is there anything? You were in power for fifteen years. This is the first dispute that has occurred since you left office. Have you provided
[Mr. Butte. 1
for it? If you have not, then why do you quarrel?

This subject is so important, and I take and have for many years taken such an interest in it, that I should like to say a word or two. This is not a party question. In the capable hands of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), it seems to have been given a turn that was an appeal to those who are prejudiced against the defence of their country.
Order.

The defence of the country is a matter which is absolutely divorced from party; it applies to both parties. I do not know the necessity for this increase in the permanent force, but I have a trust in the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mew-burn), because I have noticed since I have been in this House, his sanity and his want of impetuosity in dealing with the affairs of his office. If he says that it is essential that power should be given to call up another 5,000 men, I am going to follow him. The Bill does not say that they must be called hip; it simply gives the power. Give him a dose, for Heaven's sake.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks-

Before the hon. member begins his remarks, and in order that I shall not be obliged to call any other hon. member to order, I must remind the

Mr. Chairman, I will follow the rules as closely as I possibly can, but I must say that I am surprised that the Government should bring in a Bill at the present time having- as its object the increasing of our standing military force by 5,000 men. The war is over and we have now entered upon the period of reconstruction. The country is faced with an expenditure this year of $620,000,000, and the total revenue that is in sight, after taxing everything that can possibly be taxed, is only $280,000,000, so that $340,000,000 more will have to be raised. The Minister of Finance will have to go before the country this coming fall and borrow this money. Whether he borrows the morfey in Canada or in the United States, he will have to find it, and in view of the figures which I have quoted, is it reasonable to embark on any undertaking that will create a further deficit? I for one would rather see the Government pay the returned men a bonus of $1,000 each. This would represent paying that sum to each of 300,000 to 500,000 men, a million dollars.
One hundred million.
Well, one hundred million. I beg your pardon, Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend is wrong. Three hundred million dollars divided among 300,000 men would be $1,000 apiece.
It would be $2 apiece.

I have the figures here, although I have not looked at them very closely. Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to say to the hon. minister that if you give a bonus to these men who have given their all in the service of the country you will do more to satisfy the people than if you increase the standing military forces of the country, for such a step would only tend to excite public indignation. The prime cause of

public dissatisfaction at the present time is directly attributable to this Government, which, though allowing profiteers to make from seventy to one hundred per cent, and even as high as three hundred per cent, has helped to increase the cost of living. These soldiers who fought so nobly for the cause of the Empire are returning out of work and will find it exceedingly difficult indeed to live on the small wages which will be available unless some substantial assistance is given them. I have every respect for my hon. friend the Minister of Militia, but I would seriously urge on him the necessity of abandoning this Bill.
. If he dropped this measure the country would commend him. In any event, the present is no time to increase expenditures unnecessarily when we are faced already with $600,000,000 for the current year. When we consider that a small country like Canada has a debt of $220 per capita it is high time that we should think of taking some sane steps to reduce the expenses of the country.

friend propose to get this billion dollars which he suggests that the Government should spend in the way of bonuses to the soldiers?

It would be easier to pay

If you give these men $1,000 or $2,000 apiece it will be finished forever and the people will be satisfied.

If the proposition of
the hon. member were carried out and you gave $2,000 apiece to each man, that would mean one billion dollars. If you gave them $1,000 apiece it would be five hundred million dollars. Has the hon. member calculated the interest on this sum?

On section 2-Rates of pay of permanent force to be fixed by Governor in Council instead of by statute:

Will the minister give
an explanation of what the Government intends to do in this regard?

Major-General MEWBURN:	I said this
afternoon that my immediate concern is to recommend to the Governor in Council a very small increase in the permanent force. I made it very clear then that I did not intend to increase the force immediately to 10,000. With regard to the second subsection, we will have to increase the pay of the permanent force, and I have not determined the actual figures. For instance, in the Northwest Mounted Police the pay for a staff-sergeant, per day is $3.25 including allowances; that of a warrant officer in the permanent forces is only $2.30, and the private in the permanent force, including field allowance receives $1.10. The constable receives, the first year, $2 a day.
My idea is that it might be put on the same scale as that upon which the Mounted Police now are. I had a letter from Calgary to-day, in which it is stated that the men of the permanent force are complaining that they cannot live on their pay and that it ought to be made equal to that of the Northwest Mounted Police. That is my recommendation to the Governor in Council.

Mr. Chairman, I quite agree with what the minister has said in relation to the necessity of something being done to increase the pay of the permanent force, if the men who are to be on that force are to be the class of men that the minister would desire to have. I come from a city which is the headquarters of Military District No. 3, and I should like very much to see the members of the new force of such a class as the minister would like them to be. To that end he will have to give some consideration to the question of the improvement of the barrack accommodation of the permanent force. The greater part of the life of these men is spent in barracks. Their remuneration is made up not only of the money that they receive, but of certain allowances, quarters and accommodation. The accommodation in Kingston for the use of the permanent force has been, very poor, and I would like to urge upon the minister that he take some steps to secure some of the beautiful sites situated around Kingston for barrack purposes and that he turn over for commercial purposes the present barracks in the city. While I am on the subject of remuneration, let me say that I would like to see a new scale of pay adopted for the entire permanent force. New Zealand has taken up the whole question of the permanent force and has done away with a great many of the allowances and perquisites that have for so many years been considered necessary. I would like to see a scheme of remuneration adopted by which a definite amount for the services of officers and a definite amount for the services of the men would be paid in dollars and cents, that the public could measure and understand. I would also like to see such a change made in the permanent force as would abolish the system by which the superior ranks are entitled to the services of the rank and file in such occupations as cleaning furnaces, shovelling walks, waiting on table, and, in some cases looking after children. The civilian population resent that sort of thing. It is far from dignified, it has had an unfortunate effect on the rank and file, and it lends itself to abuse. I would like to urge upon the minister that he give consideration to this point. But, I want to urge especially upon him to see if something cannot be done to improve the quarters which for a century or so have been occupied by the permanent force at Kingston, because the present barracks are the successors of a certain establishment founded by Front-enac when he landed in what is now Kingston something over two centuries ago.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word about what has been suggested by some of the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Nickle). If the Minister of Militia followed the suggestion of the hon. member and built new barracks in the city of Kingston on any one of the beautiful sites which, I confess, are numerous, he would be wasting money. There has been enough money wasted in Kingston by the Department of Public Works. We have at Barriefield a great many buildings which were erected, some of them even after the armistice was signed, and which are to-day absolutely useless. It is true that the barracks in Kingston are no better than a rathole. They have been a disgrace to the militia of Canada for as long as my memory can carry me. They should be torn down and thrown into the lake, there is no doubt in my mind as to that. If the city of Kingston had had any enterprise about it some years ago when the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) was Minister of Militia, it would have accepted the suggestion made by him, torn those buildings down and thrown them into the lake. But Kingston is proverbially slow when it comes to anything along progressive lines. The people there have been content to look

at the old rotten barracks they have there, and pride themselves on the fact that the buildings were erected years and years ago by some person who was connected with the early history of the country. They would rather continue to look at the old rathole of a barracks which has an inscription on a stone over the arch than have it interfered with in any way, because that would be laying profane hands upon a sacred piece of history. What I would sug-egst as a counter proposal to what has been suggested by the hon. member for Kingston is this: You have at Barriefield Commons a number of buildings which have been erected at enormous cost to this country and which are useless. These buildings can be made useful for barracks purposes. You have not to go very far from where these buildings are to get solid rook. If you will merely place a wall under these buildings and then veneer them with brick, you will have good buildings at a minimum of cost and you will be relieved of the worry of knowing what to do with the buildings which you have there now, which have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and which are absolutely useless at the present time. There is where your barracks ought to be. Get rid of the rathole barracks in Kingston just as quickly as you can.

I understand that we are dealing with the pay of the permanent force, and that it is proposed that the pay shall be settled by Order in Council. I think that is a mistake.

Major-General MEWBURN: It is to be approved by the Governor in Council.

Yes; Parliament is not 'to fix the scale. I think the minister will be doing the wise thing if he puts down a scale for Parliament to adopt, because there will be constant friction and trouble with the Militia Department in regard to the question of pay if that is not done. If the scale is fixed by Parliament, every soldier who enlisted in the permanent force will know what his pay is and he will know that the Governor in Council has no power to change it. It will make him more contented and it will be more satisfactory all round. Under this system you may have a strike among the members of your , permanent force, as we had in the Post Office Department, and to avoid anything of that kind I think i't would be better that the minister should make the pay of the soldiers statutory. It formerly was statutory and that system worked very well. If the minister is prepared to say how much he intends to pay them, it would be better to put it in the Act and make it a part of the law of the land.
Major-General MEWBURN: There is a good deal in what my hon. friend says, but I think it is perfectly safe to leave the matter in the hands of the Governor in Council. Everybody will admit that the old statutory provision of 75 cents a day is entirely out of the question. I do not anticipate that there will be any particular increase this year, but provision will have to be made in the Estimates probably at another session. At the present time we are paying the men $1.10 per diem, the same as the Canadian Expeditionary Force, and I feel we will have to continue that, probably to the end of this year. I am endeavouring to get the rates paid in the United States, Great Britain, New Zealand and Australia. At present we do not anticipate that the pay will be increased beyond that of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police-the rates paid to the two forces will probably run together. On section 116-"aotiiary" defined.

This section as it appears in the Bill and as it passed the
Senate, was found to operate harshly upon a number of societies that were being served by actuaries who were not able to measure up to the standard set out therein. When the Bill was before the Committee on Banking and Commerce the position
10 p.m. of matters was explained by the member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier).	There were
originally four societies affected by the legislation as it appeared before the Senate -the Maccabees, the Artisans, the Canadian Order of Foresters, and I think the Alliance Nationale. I do not know whether there	were any others, but
these	four at least	were affected,and	the section as	it stood deprived them of the services of the actuaries who had been serving them for a number of years. It was intended by the amendment made by the Committee on Banking and Commerce to relieve the condition with respect to all these societies, but the section as it passed that committee failed to give relief in any instance except that of the Artisans. I would therefore suggest to the Minister of Finance that an amended section be adopted which would give the relief which I believe it was the intention of the Committee on Banking and Commerce to afford. I would therefore propose to strike out section 116 as amended by the Banking and Commerce Committee and substitute the following:
116. The term " actuary " in this part means a Fellow of the Institute of Actuaries of Great Britain, the Faculty of Actuaries in Scotland, or the Actuarial Society of America; Provided, however, that an actuary who for a period of not less than five years preceding the date of the passing of this Act has been serving any fraternal benefit society transacting business in Canada on the said date as its actuary, and who has been in active -practice as an actuary for a period of not less than twenty-five years prior to the said date, may, for the purposes of this Act, with the consent of the superintendent, be continued as the actuary of any fraternal benefit society by which at the said date he is employed as actuary.
The changes which this amendment would cover are principally the reduction of the period of service from thirty to twenty-five years; and, also, it would give to any actuary who has been serving a society doing business in Canada for five years, the right to continue to serve not only that society, but any other society that he is at present serving. That is an important change from the amendment made by the Committee on Banking and Commerce, for the reason that some societies are being served by actuaries of more than twenty-
3P88

five years' experience who have not been serving them for five years, but who have been serving other societies doing business in Canada for a longer period than five years. It will be admitted that a service of twentydive years is just as safe a guarantee of ability as a service of thirty years. If an actuary has not developed in twenty-five years the qualifications which would entitle him to be considered a satisfactory officer under the provisions of this Act, it is extremely unlikely that five years' additional service would make him any more efficient or trustworthy for the business that would devolve upon him under the Act.
