On motion of Sir Thomas White, Bill No. 143, to amend the Business Profits- War Tax Act, 1916, was read the second time, arfd the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the "Chair.
Bill reported without amendment.

On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance), Bill No. 144, to amend The Income War Tax Act, 1917, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the -chair.
On section 2-income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I promised the committee, when the resolution preceding the Bill was under consideration, that I would increase the age limit of each child in .respect of which the taxpayer is granted exemption of $200. To that end I move that the word " eighteen " be substituted for the word " sixteen " in the second line of paragraph (b), subsection 2 of this section.
This will be in addition to the statutory exemption?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Amendment agreed to.

I find it somewhat difficult to understand the meaning of paragraph (e). It reads:

(e) In determining the income no deduction shall be allowed in respect of personal and living expenses, and in cases in which personal and living expenses form part of the profit, gain or remuneration of the taxpayer, the same shall he assessed as income for the purposes of this Act.
It seems to me that there is a lack of clearness in the first part of that paragraph. It is quite evident that no one has the right to deduct his personal and living expenses from income before he declares it for the purposes of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just to make it clear that that deduction must not be made. All kinds of representations are put forward with a view to securing a reduction of the income assessment, and we want to make it perfectly clear that the full net income must be assessed. As to the second part of the paragraph, with reference to cases in which personal and living expenses form part of the profit, gain, or remuneration of the taxpayer, there are many who derive as a substantial part of their income the benefits of house or living expenses, and it would not be fair that these should not be taken into account.
Let us say that a Presbyterian minister gets $4,000 a year and his manse, would he be expected to pay income tax on the rental of the manse?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Unless he was
specially exempted, I think that he would. But not very many Presbyterian ministers receive $4,000.
There are six, Mr. *Chairman. A man does not have to pay income tax on the rental of his house when he lives in his own house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

There is an anomaly
there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend. The man who rents a house has to pay rental; the man who owns his house has the benefit of that ownership so far as income tax is concerned. That is something to which I shall give attention at the next session if possible. It raises a very difficult question, because allowance would have to be made on some basis for the capital invested in the house. All kinds of anomalies would arise in the administration of any such provision; that is
one reason why, generally speaking, it is not in income taxation measures.

Suppose a commercial traveller gets $5,000 a year and hotel and personal expenses. Under paragraph (e) he should pay income tax on those living expenses, which are really part of his remuneration. I suggest that there should be something in the Act to indicate the way in which that should be collected.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, to lay down regulations; we have to deal with individual cases as they occur. It has been brought to my attention by men who have certain living allowances that when they travel they are out of pocket; their allowances are not adequate, and they are put to other expense. Of course, they have the inconvenience of being away from home.
So have we.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know, but a
great deal is expected of us; we cannot put our services on a money basis. The department, in the case of commercial travellers, has not added anything to the income by reason of the living expenses allowed. Whether right or not, that is the policy we have adopted.
If I may interject, the living expenses of a traveller certainly come under this clause of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They do, and this was intended to cover cases of which tha,t is an example, but whether we would be able to add on the full amount they are allowed, I am unable to say in advance. We would have to take all the facts into consideration. A man might prove that he was out of pocket; that his expenses were much more than he was allowed, and you would have to deal with each case on its merits. My experience is that income tax assessment is by no means as exact a science as algebra.

May I make this suggestion with all respect to the minister?- that if he is going to go at this income tax in this empiric sort olf way, taking merely cases as they arise, it will be a very long and unsatisfactory business. Some general principle should be laid down, say, that a commercial traveller should be assessed on say two-thirds of the living allowance given him. I quite understand that you

cannot approximate it very closely, hut you can get some idea, and the Government should have some regulation, so that the scrupulous man who charges himself with all the living allowance which he gets from his house and pays income tax upon it, should not be under a disadvantage as compared with the other man with a more elastic conscience who says: "Well, I get $50, or $100, or $250 a month as living allowance from my house, but after all I have to spend considerably more than that," and so does not return it at all. Unless the minister and his hardworking commissioner are prepared to take up the case of every single traveller who pays income tax, which procedure would cause an immense amount of work, it would be wise to lay down some general principle which would roughly deal with the situation.

I should like to call the attention of the minister to a complaint from the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and particularly from a large number of railway Irainmen in the city of Stratford. They complain that, in case of an engineer, conductor, fireman and brakeman, they are forced, by virtue of their occupation, to take long runs, say to the city of Buffalo, where they are compelled to remain over, probably a whole day or more until the return train is made up They are all forced from their homes, and they have to stay at rather expensive hotels. These men are out of the class that one would call the wealthy class, and although they are men of small means, they are bound to pay a tax under*- the schedule that is laid down now. They complain that while they have to keep up their own homes in Stratford where they live, with all attendant expenses, they are practically compelled to keep up a home in a hotel while they are away for probably two days in the week, or even three. This amounts to a very severe penalty upon these men, because they do not really get the income that would become taxable if you allowed them anything for the extra expenses to which they are put. I have been asked to draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance and I do so in the hope-because I appreciate that the same may be true of commercial travellers-that some equitable principle may be arrived at, if not now, at some time in the future, by which a deserving case of this kind will be exempted from a taxation which

bears rather heavily under the circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We shall be glad to take under consideration what has been said and will see if some regulation can be made to meet the circumstances. A commercial traveller receives his railway fare and hotel bills, and his hotel bill might reasonably be added to his income unless something exceptional can be set up, and I do not at the moment know what could be so set up. With regard to engineers and conductors, my hon. friend will see at once the difficulty that would arise there, in the different standards of living. One man might go to an expensive hotel and another to a less expensive one, and it is exceedingly difficult to lay down a regulation to meet a case of that kind. The Commissioner of Taxation has not been able up to date to see his wqy clear to make any allowance. This discussion all goes to show the difficulty of administering with scrupulous fairness an income taxation measure, but notwithstanding that difficulty every effort should be made to carry out the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree with my hon-. friend. The reason why we referred to commercial travellers was because it was an obvious- case, because they do travel and are allowed expenses. The hon. member says precisely what I had in mind, namely, that it was very difficult to lay 'down rules, because as I pointed out, the expense allowances might really not be adequate. My experience has been that, whenever I have been travelling where I have had a certain allowance, I have been out of pocket, but others may be more fortunate.
The minister should also bear in mind the case of the man who works on- a commission basis and whose entire income will be rated for income tax purposes.
I should like to fix in the minister's mind the distinction between a railway man and a commercial traveller.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Their cases are entirely opposite.
The ^railwayman has to pay this expense out of his own pocket always.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understand that.

I understand we are at section 2, and I want to draw the attention of the minister to paragraph (f) which says:
(f) Deficits or losses sustained in transactions entered into for profit but not connected with the chief business, trade, profession or occupation of the taxpayer shall not be deducted from income derived from the chief business, trade, profession or occupation of the taxpayer in determining his taxable income.
It will be very difficult 'to determine what the chief business of some firms is. I know a firm that is engaged in the investment business, lumber business and grocery business. I know their business very intimately, but it would be difficult for me to tell which is their chief business. I know another firm engaged in the shipping business and also in a machine shop business. I do not see much use in the word " chief." Why not eliminate it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the word "chief" is necessary to emphasize the intention. The difficulty we encounter is this: A man has an income from his occupation of say, $10,000, and he engages in stock speculation and loses two or three
thousand dollars and desires to deduct that. We will not allow him to do so. If a firm engages in half a dozen different businesses and takes a flyer on the side, we will not allow them to set up any loss in respect of that. It is surprising how often the contention is set up that something should be allowed for losses on the side. The department will administer the section in the sense that "chief occupation" means the /occupation which is actually and bona fide engaged in from day to day, and no deduction will be allowed for losses incurred in transactions, not connected therewith, such as stock transactions. Not long ago it was brought to my attention that a man who had a large income took it into his head that he could become a successful farmer. They say when a man does fancy farming he is an "agriculturist," as distinguished a "farmer" who does real farming and makes money. The "agriculturist" nearly always loses money, and we do not propose to let him set up any loss in this enterprise. We will assess him on his income. We do not desire to discourage him from going into farming, but do not think he should set up such losses against a substantial income he derives in the city.

I desire to call the minister's attention to a matter which it seems there is a general fear to touch upon. Members of Parliament pay a tax on $2,500,, and I know of cases where members find a deficit in the personal budget when they return home. The living expenses in Ottawa take the whole of the indemnity and sometimes more, according to the length of the session. I know that this is a delicate matter, but I am not afraid to touch, it. People ought to know that not only do we not receive anything for our services here, but that while we are here we have to pay a tax, for the pleasure of being here, on money that most of us do not receive any real benefit from. I think there ought to be an allowance for living expenses. It cannot be argued that there is a great saving in the individual home, for our families have to be provided for at home while we pay separate expenses here, and we are actually out of pocket in the final result. It is not right, and whatever the country may think of my statement I speak my mind about the matter. I think, that as a matter of principle, we ought not to be called upon to pay taxes on money that does not benefit us as a matter of fact, because we would not spend that much at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like
very much to meet the views of my hon. friend because I realize that there is' a great deal of justice in what he says. The sessional allowance is in the nature of an indemnity; it is not intended to be in the nature of income but to indemnify the member against his expenses in attending Parliament and also against demands that might be made upon him from day to day as a public man. When I had to do with assessments in Toronto I recall that the parliamentary allowance was looked upon as indemnity. I think one of the members of this House, the late Mr. Lancaster, brought the matter up-I am speaking now about municipal income assessment-and my recollection is that it was held by a county judge to be an indemnity and not a part of salary. On the other hand, I think it would be the view of the majority of members of Parliament that, notwithstanding the force of my hon. friend's contentions, at a time like this the public would not be likely to approve of members of Parliament escaping taxation upon their sessional indemnity. If the public could be made to realize all that is involved, they would not object so strongly, but it is almost impossible to make them realize it, and members will have to look upon this as one of the necessary sacrifices they make in connection with the public position. However, there is a great deal of weight in what my hon. friend puts forward.
I do not want the indemnity to be exempt, but I think a certain amount should be allowed for living expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would give rise to difficulties also. The living expenses of one member would differ from those of another, and that is a matter that might he misunderstood by the public. The amount involved is not large, and I think that members on the whole would rather be assessed than not. But if there is any widespread'opinion on the matter, I should like to have an expression of it.
There will not be. People are afraid to talk.
In the event of a speculator making, say $10,000 on a transaction, how will that be treated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Gains or losses in transactions on the side are disregarded, because the losses usually offset the gains.

I am told that in stock transactions ninety per cent are usually losses.

Does not a man pay
income tax on a successful stock transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It works both ways. He pays on his dividend, of course. But if he takes a flyer and makes something, next week he might take another flyer and lose it.

In subsection 5 on page 3,	" dividends and shareholders'
bonuses," the Act provides that dividends or bonuses paid to shareholders by a corporation on or after the first of January, 1917, shall be taxable as income. The Bank of Nova Scotia has a surplus twice as large as its capital. If they decided to distribute that surplus ot any part of it at any time, it having bexn accumulated prior to 1917, would it be taxable against the shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will observe a date, the purpose of which is to give the Act a start. A reserve prior to the date mentioned, 1st January, 1917, is treated as capital, and if there was a distribution of that it would be regarded as capital distribution rather than income. If they have added to that reserve since and made a distribution, the dividend derived from that would be assessable.
On section 3, subseotion (a)-Normal tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It has been
drawn to our attention that there are some unmarried people wh o have dependent fathers or mothers, or both. Take the case of a young woman earning $1,600 a year and having to maintain an invalid father or mother.
We have" thought it well to classify such a person with married persons, widows and widowers with dependent children. We exempt up to the extent of $2,000 married persons and widows or widowers having dependent children. We want to put into that class unmarried people who have a father or mother depending upon them for support. To accomplish that I beg to move that:
The section-page 4, line 1, be amended by inserting after word " children " the words " and persons who are not supporting dependent brothers or sisters under the age of eighteen years or a dependent parent or parents."
I think that is just. It was drawn to my attention by some one.

I have been asked to draw the minister's attention to the case of unmarried women. Why should an unmarried woman have to pay a larger tax than a married woman? Take the case of two sisters, one of whom is unmarried. They both get the same income; we will say that it is $4,000 a year. The married one has her husband to support her and she has her $4,000 for pin or pocket money. The unmarried one has no husband to support her. She gets the same amount but she has to pay on $3,000, whereas the married one only has to pay on $2,000 simply because she is married. What is the reason of that? It is regarded as an inequality, a discrimination against the unmarried women, and some women have asked me to draw the matter to the attention of the minister. I am quite in sympathy with taxing the unmarried man, but I am not in favour of taxing the unmarried woman to a greater extent than the married woman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason underlying the distinction is that married people are supposed to have greater responsibilities towards children and the upkeep of the home. That is the only reason I can give my hon. friend. There may be some anomalies in the administration of the Act, but the principle is sound.
The husband is responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The wife may have to keep the house.

It is not so ordinarily. The husband may be a trial to the wife, but usually he is a means of financial gain, and it is ridiculous, as my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) so well pointed out, that Miss B. with an income of $3,000, let us say, has to pay on $2,000, while her sister, Mrs. C., with exactly the same income, and with a husband to rely upon, has to pay on only $1,000. That is an anomaly that the minister should correct. It is not reasonable, it is unjust, and the idea that the minister gives that children are to be supported, does not hold water. As a rule the husband maintains the family; the wife has, as a rule, the income for herself unless she wishes to join forces with her husband to live in a style more luxurious than they would be living in had the family to depend entirely upon the earnings of the husband. Under these conditions it is unjust to tax an unmarried woman more heavily than a married woman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To give effect to what is suggested would mean that the unmarried woman with no responsibility would have to be exempt up to $2,000, whereas the man without responsibility is exempt to the amount of $1,000. I think that a woman without responsibility and having an income of $2,000 might very well be assessed. The real question is as to whether there should be one exemption only in the case of husband and wife.
I think there should.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a good deal to be said for that, and it has been discussed pro and con. But we would not be justified in stating that a man. should be exempt to the extent of $1,000 while a woman with no responsibility should be exempt up to $2,000, because a man usually has more responsibilities than a woman has.

Instead of bringing the unmarried woman's exemption up to $2,000 it might be proper to bring the married woman's exemption down to $1,000; or you might do what the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has been urging the Minister of Finance to do for some years- regard the husband's and wife's income as a joint income and give one exemption in relation to it. That would possibly do away with this difficulty, because the present situation is not Jair, and, I think, rather works to the disadvantage of the revenue.
Let her marry.
The hon. member (Mr. Bureau) suggests: Let the girl marry. That may not be within the power of the young lady herself.
Should that exemption not be extended to the case of unmarried persons having grandparents to support? There are many such cases.
I think grandparents otight to he put in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a good deal of sympathy with the grandparents. How would it do to add, after the word " parents," " grandparent or grandparents?"
Or make it " ascendants in the direct line."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, no. I beg to move;
That the words " grandparent or grandparents " he added.
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.

Before talcing up the next clause I would like to call attention to another class of people who are escaping taxation and I think it is unfortunate that they should do so.
There is a large class of people, more particularly in the large centres of Toronto and Montreal, employed as operators in garment factories. They are foreigners, and their incomes are very large. Those unacquainted with the business have no idea of the large sums these people earn from week to week, from month to month, and from year to year. They are a wandering class of people, and I am told by those who know, that their incomes range from $50 to $90 or $100 per week. I realize the difficulty in reaching that class, and therefore I would suggest to the Minister of Finance that the employers of these people collect from them a certain amount each week to be retained and paid pver to the income tax department, making the employers responsible for the collection. I am morally certain it would secure a large addition to the revenue of the country if these people could be reached in any way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We call for returns from the employer in all these cases where over $1,000 a year is paid in wages. I know that what my hon. friend says as to the amount these people receive is correct, or substantially so. The fact was incidentally drawn to my attention not very long ago that some of these garment makers made very high rates of pay. I do not say that they do not earn that pay, no doubt they do. They must be very expert, and earnings of $60 or $70 a week may not be out of the way, although they may appear large for the work that is done. At any rate we d-o get returns from all these merchant tailors and others.

These people cannot be assessed under their yearly income, they work from day to day, and week to week, and they change around from place to place. In spite of that they are a class of people who earn very high remuneration for the work they do. If the department simply aocepts the statement of the employers as to the yearly income it will not reach these people at all. You will have to get at them in another way, obtain returns of their weekly income, and see that their employers secure the taxes that these workers should be called upon to pay.
t Sir Thomas White.I

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am glad to have the matter drawn to the attention of the Commissioner of Taxation.
I now wish to move an amendment-, by inserting the following clause immediately before clause 4:
4. Section five of the said Act is amended by adding thereto the following paragraph:-
" (i) Income derived from any pension granted to any member of His Majesty's military, naval or air forces for any disability suffered by the pensioner while serving in any of His Majesty's forces during the war that began in August, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, and the income derived from any pension granted to any dependent relative of any person w'ho was killed or suffered any disability while serving in the said forces in the said war."
I think that meets the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) and concurred in. by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux).

Amendment agreed to.
On section 5-books of account must be kept:
Will the minister explain what kind of books he will require for the farming community?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will observe that " adequate " books are called for.
That is pretty broad.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provision has some flexibility and it is in the discretion of the minister whether he will call for books or not. It would seem to me impossible to require the farming community to keep books, although I think many farmers do so. I have pointed out some difficulties in assessing the farming community, but nevertheless we will have to do the best we can.

The minister told us that in a previous section which has been concurred in a penalty has been provided for not making the required return. Is it the purpose of the department to take any steps to deal with defaulters?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amended provision will enable us to do so. Under the Act as it stands the only thing we can do is to summon the delinquent party before a magistrate, and that is not a very satisfactory way of dealing with the matter. I

think the experience of governments in administering the income tax is that nothing brings payment so promptly as a penalty. That principle is observed in the case of municipal taxation; if you do not pay your taxes promptly a certain percentage is added. The income tax law being on the statute books we must enforce it, and there must be a penalty to enable the department to do so. It is very much better not to have such a law in operation if we do not assess in full. As far as we are concerned we are going to give the Act a very strict interpretation.	-
Mr-. PEDLOW: If the department will grant a discount I think it will be more
effective in securing prompt payment than a penalty. I have in mind the experience of the municipality of the town of Renfrew.
And the city of Ottawa.
The town of Renfrew gets on the specified date almost the entire amount of taxation due, by allowing discount for prompt payment.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, and amendments read the first and second time, and concurred in.
